articles.title_orig: Mexico's week in review: Sheinbaum in China, Rodríguez at the mic and a kingpin behind bars
articles.title_zh: Mexico's week in review: Sheinbaum in China, Rodríguez at the mic and a kingpin behind bars
articles.content_orig:
President Claudia Sheinbaum spent most of the week in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. That left Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez running the mañaneras from Monday on. The Minnesota Vikings, meanwhile, were pumping thin air into a chamber in the Midwest to prepare for Sunday night’s kickoff in Mexico City.
It was a relatively calm week at home while the president was abroad. That changed Friday night, when Mexican special forces captured an alleged drug kingpin on the FBI’s Top 10 Most Wanted list, sparking violence in Sinaloa.
Didn’t have time to catch Mexico’s top stories of the week of Nov. 16? Here’s what you missed.
Sheinbaum left Mexico City’s airport at 11 p.m. on Saturday for a 12:35 a.m. flight to Tijuana. She then boarded China Southern Airlines flight CZ8032 to Shenzhen. It was another commercial flight, in keeping with the austerity symbolism started by her predecessor. She arrived at 11:30 a.m. Monday local time and went straight to the Tequila Coyote’s restaurant to meet Mexicans living in China, whom she called “extraordinary.” The economy-class journey also struck a chord online : Bloomberg reported that a hashtag about her arrival was seen 10 million times on Weibo.
In a 13-minute speech at the APEC CEO Summit on Tuesday, Sheinbaum told more than 2,000 business and political representatives that Mexico “guarantees conditions for investment.” She said the government and private companies expect to invest US $432 billion in infrastructure under Plan México between 2024 and 2030. She also described the plan as having a “humanist vision.”
Mexico News Daily noted that foreign direct investment hit a record of almost $35 billion in the first half of 2026, though growth was only 2.1%. Insecurity, USMCA uncertainty and the recent judicial reform are seen as deterrents. On Thursday, she gave a four-minute address at the Leaders’ Meeting, calling this “a decisive moment for humanity.” Mexico will host APEC in 2028.
Sheinbaum told Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday that her visit marks “a new era” in bilateral ties, focused on science, technology, clean energy and health. Neither side’s readout mentioned Mexico’s new tariffs on Chinese goods. She also revealed she had asked Xi for a panda for Chapultepec Zoo.
She also met Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney that day, and both reaffirmed support for renewing the USMCA. Carney said bilateral trade is up 18% this year.
On Wednesday came the one many were watching: a roughly 20-minute meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump, her first formal in-person talks with him. Sheinbaum said trade negotiations are “very far along” but gave no timeline for a deal. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said 56 technical meetings have been held. Trump’s recent tariff threat over the migrant caravan went unmentioned, and the two agreed to meet again at next month’s G20 summit at Mar-a-Lago.
She also met leaders from Vietnam, Australia, Singapore and Peru, plus the IMF’s Kristalina Georgieva. At her closing press conference, Sheinbaum called the trip “very productive and very successful” but said Mexico has no plans for a free trade agreement with China.
With the president away, Interior Minister Rodríguez led this week’s morning press conferences. On Monday, the mañanera featured World Bank data showing that Mexico’s monetary poverty rate fell from 35.3% in 2018 to 21.1% in 2025, with 17.3 million fewer people in poverty projected by the end of 2026. Officials also touted a CB Global Data poll putting Sheinbaum’s approval at 69.8%, the highest in Latin America.
Sheinbaum joined Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday’s mañanera by video link, and on Thursday, Rodríguez praised her boss’s “composure” and “firmness, without confrontation or subservience.”
An APEC report showed that Mexico ranks fourth among APEC economies in the share of exports that are medium- and high-tech goods, at 70.6%. Only Taiwan, Hong Kong and South Korea rank higher. Mexico sits ahead of China (61.6%), the United States (46.5%) and Canada (31.7%). APEC projects regional growth of 3.4% this year and 3.1% in 2027.
Hours after landing from China, Sheinbaum presided over the parade marking the 116th anniversary of the Mexican Revolution. She invoked the 1917 Constitution and defended democratic freedoms. She also accused political opponents and foreign interests of trying to weaken her administration and delegitimize the 2027 midterms. Pageant floats and military contingents then rolled through the Zócalo and down Paseo de la Reforma.
The peso sank past 19 per dollar on Thursday, hitting 19.04, its weakest level in 17 months. Bloomberg tied the move to Banxico’s dovish stance, after a 25-basis-point cut to 6.25%, and expectations of another Fed hike in December. That would narrow the interest-rate gap that supports the carry trade. The peso is down about 5.5% this year.
The November MND Peso Index™ offers some context. It found the peso 4.2% undervalued at 18.67 per dollar, versus a 0.7% undervaluation in October. The swing was driven almost entirely by depreciation.
The Pan American Health Organization revoked the measles-free status of Mexico, the United States and Bolivia after 12 months of continuous transmission. Canada lost its status a year earlier. Mexico has recorded 20,601 cases over 2025 and 2026, but only 14 are currently active, down from a February peak of 1,314. The government aims to end the outbreak in the second half of 2027 and regain recognition in 2028.
A caravan of about 1,500 migrants left Tapachula last Tuesday, and Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexican goods if it isn’t stopped. By Tuesday, it had shrunk to 781 people in Mapastepec, Chiapas, as migration officials urged people to go home. On Thursday, Rodríguez responded to U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s remarks by saying Mexico “will continue detaining” people involved in smuggling.
José Luis Abarca, Iguala’s mayor during the 2014 Ayotzinapa tragedy, was sentenced to 60 years on Nov. 10 by a federal judge in Tamaulipas. He and 25 co-defendants, including the police chief, were convicted of six counts of aggravated homicide and attempted murder. Those charges stem from the attack on a bus carrying the Los Avispones soccer team. Abarca is already serving 20- and 92-year sentences. His lawyer argued police control had been ceded to then-Gov. Ángel Aguirre.
Friday night’s big news came from Sinaloa. Mexican special forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” and two other leaders of his organization.
Mexican special forces capture top FBI fugitive ‘El Chapo Isidro,’ unleashing a night of fire in Sinaloa
The FBI lists Meza Flores on its Top 10 Most Wanted list and had offered up to US $5 million for information leading to his arrest. Agents came under fire from gunmen using explosives during the raid in Guasave, according to the Defense Ministry. Violence erupted afterward, with civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game and vehicles burning on a highway near Los Mochis. The Mexican government said U.S. intelligence helped, giving few details. The three were flown to Mexico City.
The aftermath in Sinaloa is the story to watch, as violence following the capture may not end quickly. On trade, Sheinbaum and Trump are due to meet again at the G20 in Florida next month. Sheinbaum has said talks are “very far along,” but no deal date has been set, and the U.S. has still not agreed to any tariff reductions for Mexican automobiles, steel or aluminum . Financial markets, meanwhile, will be watching the Fed’s December meeting and Banxico’s decision on Dec. 17 for clues about whether the peso’s slide continues. Back at the Estadio Azteca, the Vikings and 49ers will find out Sunday whether their different altitude strategies paid off.

articles.title_orig: Treasury secretary rules out further restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China
articles.title_zh: Treasury secretary rules out further restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday that no further restrictions on the sale of older Nvidia chips to China are needed following the Trump administration's move earlier this week to block China's remote access to the latest semiconductors.
The ability of Chinese tech firms to access Nvidia’s technology came under scrutiny after CEO Jensen Huang stepped down amid allegations of his affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that uses advanced chips to generate computing power that Chinese firms access remotely.
“The proper chip restrictions are in place,” Bessent said in an interview with CNBC after returning from a trip to Asia with President Donald Trump . “And the remote access has been curtailed.”
Bessent's comments came a day after the House Foreign Affairs Committee released details of the Commerce Department's approval of the sales of more than 850,000 chips from Nvidia and its competitor AMD to Chinese companies. The Pentagon has identified some of those companies as having ties to the Chinese military.
The report tracked applications from Nvidia to sell its H200 chips — one of its more powerful products, though not the most advanced — and AMD's applications to sell its roughly comparable MI325X chip to companies that are either located or headquartered in China, or entities with parent companies based in China.
The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security approved the export, re-export, or transfer of 879,868 of these chips to companies with Chinese ties across 21 license applications as of May 11, 2026, the report said. Nvidia and AMD had requested to sell a cumulative total of more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese-tied companies across those applications, per the report.
The approvals, which don't necessarily indicate completed sales, included 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent and its subsidiaries, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, according to the report. Each of those companies has been identified by the Defense Department as having ties to the Chinese military.
The report shows the Commerce Department has a “long track record of transparency with Congress about licensing activity for the H200 and equivalent chips, including both approvals and rejections,” a spokesperson for the Bureau of Industry and Security said in a statement Friday.
The spokesperson said the Commerce Department's approach to H200 licensing is based on a rule in the Federal Register that was published in January. The rule imposes “significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial,” the spokesperson said.
An Nvidia spokesperson said in a statement Friday that the “limited shipments we made under the H200 program were legal and authorized” by the BIS. “The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes," the company spokesperson said.
Earlier this week, Nvidia said it was no longer shipping H200 chips to China. The spokesperson said Friday that shipments had stopped despite prior approvals.
AMD said it complies with U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains “rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations” in a statement from a spokesperson Friday. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity,” the spokesperson said.
Chinese technology firms have been bracing for impacts on their ambitious AI development plans as scrutiny mounts on export controls in the U.S.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under intense scrutiny himself in the wake of the turmoil following the Huang affair. Last week, Bessent said he was frustrated with the Commerce Department’s delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed International, which is under investigation by the U.S. for potentially diverting restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. A former executive at the company who allegedly had an affair with Huang was reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being a spy for China.
In an unusually public rebuke of a fellow Cabinet member, Bessent said his department wanted to place export controls on Megaspeed, but Commerce was in charge of the matter.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Trump said he has “not lost confidence” in Lutnick. Calling him a “different kind of guy," Trump said he “has a natural business instinct” and has “done a very good job.”
Huamani reported from Los Angeles. Associated Press writer Meg Kinnard contributed from Columbia, South Carolina.

articles.title_orig: El Salvador’s Bukele seeks third term that could keep him in power until 2033
articles.title_zh: El Salvador’s Bukele seeks third term that could keep him in power until 2033
articles.content_orig:
El Salvadorâs popular and ironfisted president, Nayib Bukele, formally registered his candidacy for a third term Thursday, setting the stage for elections in February that he is expected to win.
Since entering office in 2019, Bukele, 45, has found widespread support at home and from some quarters abroad for his aggressive crackdown on organized crime and a steep reduction in homicides. But he has been widely criticized for curtailing civil liberties, sweeping up alleged gang members without due process, repressing political dissent and dismantling democratic institutions.
He has successfully consolidated his power in what has become a de facto one-party state. Last year, Bukeleâs allies in the legislature changed the countryâs constitution to allow a president to serve an unlimited number of terms . If he wins next yearâs elections, he would remain president until 2033.
Speaking before cheering crowds Thursday after registering his candidacy at the countryâs electoral tribunal, Bukele said that âsome international media say there isnât democracy in El Salvador.â
âI tell them, no, no, no, there wasnât democracy in El Salvador before,â he said.
Bukele is launching his candidacy as he pursues a gang battle abroad, in Haiti, where he has deployed about 2,500 Salvadoran troops after four Salvadoran aviation technicians went missing during a gang ambush while supporting a United Nations-backed international force. This week, large crowds poured into the streets in Haiti to praise and thank Bukele.
President Donald Trump said Friday that Democrats, including Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, have called about bipartisan immigration efforts and that he is open to the possibility.
âIt was a very productive call,â Trump said at a White House news conference of his exchange with Hinojosa,   adding, âI think weâll be able to work something out.â
Hinojosa told the Texas Tribune she called Trump last weekend to discuss border security and explain why Texans near Big Bend National Park prefer electronic monitoring to a wall .
âHe understands my commitment to keeping a secure border,â said Hinojosa, who grew up on the border. âI reached out to him to make sure that he had a direct line to me, and it was a very positive conversation.â
On Thursday, Hinojosa met the stateâs border sheriffs and told Fox News, âWe need the federal government to put more resources along the border,â noting that Texas has spent $20 billion on border security, including GOP Gov. Greg Abbottâs Operation Lone Star, which she told The Washington Post last week she is reviewing to determine its legality. She told Fox that ICEâs violent interior immigration enforcement âneeds to end.â
âWe have had people killed in the streets,â she said. âI will not facilitate that. Even President Trump has acknowledged that has gone too far.â
A necropsy on Fiona, the Cincinnati Zooâs beloved hippo who died Thursday , showed that a knit hat she had ingested had traveled so far into her intestines that there was no way to surgically remove it.
In a statement Friday, zoo officials said their veterinary staff âtried everything they couldâ after Fiona swallowed a knit hat that accidentally ended up in her habitat almost two weeks ago.
The hat made its way to the middle of Fionaâs small intestine, about 25 feet beyond the final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines, zoo officials said.
There was no way to reach the hat with upper and lower endoscopy, and laparoscopic surgery was not possible, given where the hat was located, said Mike Wenninger, the zooâs director of animal health.
âOpen incision in a hippo that size â with an incision thatâs that long â would have been a death sentence for her, so the only option we had was supportive care, and unfortunately it wasnât enough for her,â Wenninger said in a video Friday.
Fionaâs unexpected death came as a shock to millions who had followed her journey since she was born six weeks premature in 2017. Since her death, mourners have been leaving flowers, cards and even watermelons â a special treat Fiona used to get on her birthday â at a makeshift memorial at the zoo.
Men made up 71 percent of the self-directed Vanguard investors who bought shares in Anthropic on the artificial intelligence companyâs first day of trading on the Nasdaq.
The major investment company said about 15,400 people, or 0.22 percent of the roughly 7 million self-directed investors who have used Vanguard for more than four months, purchased Anthropic on its first day of trading.
Of those, nearly three-fourths were men, though men make up only 55 percent of all Vanguard investors.
Still, SpaceX outpaced newcomer Anthropic â nearly 0.5 percent of self-directed investors bought shares in Elon Muskâs space company on its first day of trading in June.
The median buyer in Anthropic invested about 1 percent of their portfolio in the AI company, which makes the chatbot Claude. And the median amount of stock bought was about $1,950, Vanguard said.
Some buyers wagered heavily on the companyâs success: About 2 percent of them put more than half their portfolio into the stock.
Anthropic is one of the first of the new generation of AI companies to hit the public markets, raising about $79 billion from new investors in its initial sale.
âGrand Theft Auto VIâ generated $3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day Thursday, Rockstar Games said Friday. The studio called it the biggest entertainment launch in history, a record that spans film, music and video games.
Rockstar said it sold 32.5 million copies before the game was even out, a preorder record. Before its release, the game had sold almost half as much as the best-selling album in recorded music history, Michael Jacksonâs âThriller.â
Critics greeted the game with a 99 out of 100 on Metacritic, making it the highest-rated video game of all time. The Washington Post review called it â an astonishing American epic. â
The series breaks its own record as the fastest-selling media product of all time. In 2013, âGrand Theft Auto Vâ hit that record, generating $1 billion in sales after three days. At the worldwide box office, âAvengers: Endgameâ took five days to reach $1 billion in 2019. Christopher Nolanâs âThe Odysseyâ reached that mark in three weeks this summer.
âWe are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldnât be more excited to share this moment with you,â Sam Houser, the studioâs president and founder, said in a statement.
President Donald Trump on Friday defended ousted Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, calling for his reinstatement at the company after news broke that the tech scion had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
âHeâs a good man. By the way, heâs a man â while weâre at it. He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person,â Trump said Friday at a news conference following his trip to Asia. ââ¦ I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. You know, weâre a country of second chances.â
The Washington Post reported Monday that Nvidiaâs board was not considering reinstating Huang.
Huang, who has acknowledged the affair, has agreed to testify before Congress next month over whether Nvidia allowed Chinese companies to access its advanced chips despite U.S. export restrictions. Huang has a close relationship with Trump.
The president said Friday that it was important for the United States to protect its âbrilliant people,â like Huang.
âI think the company, if they were smart, theyâd take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work,â Trump said.
He likened his defense of the Nvidia co-founder to his support for Elon Musk, the founder of Tesla, SpaceX and xAI.
âYou know, I came to Elonâs defense in my first term very strongly,â Trump said, without elaborating on the reason

articles.title_orig: China, Russia and US historic talks: What comes next?
articles.title_zh: China, Russia and US historic talks: What comes next?
articles.content_orig:
A Rohingya refugee waves Myanmar's national flag as he waits for the arrival of U.N. General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman at a refugee camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 20, 2026.
The world’s top international court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority, more than a million of whom remain displaced.
The verdict , issued Thursday, is the first time a state has been found responsible for committing genocide in the history of the International Court of Justice, which was established in 1945. In a weekslong military campaign in 2017, Myanmar forces killed at least 10,000 people, including up to 2,109 children under five, and forced more than 700,000 others to flee the country’s northern Rakhine State.
The landmark decision could have significant implications for the legal treatment of cases brought under the 1948 Genocide Convention, Melanie O’Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia Law School, tells TIME. That includes South Africa’s pending case alleging that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza , where Israeli forces have killed tens of thousands of people over the past three years.
A spokesperson for Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing told reporters on Friday that the ruling is “unfair.” Min Aung Hlaing was the military’s commander in chief during the 2017 operation.
“It was not a decision made unanimously,” spokesperson Khine Khine Soe said, pointing out that six of the 15 judges dissented. She did not say whether Myanmar would comply with the ruling.
Myanmar’s military junta-backed government denied committing genocide during the proceedings.
Read More: Myanmar’s Dictator Wants to Rebuild Ties With the West
The National Unity Government, a parallel government formed after Myanmar’s 2021 military coup, said on Thursday that it respects the judgment.
For the Rohingya, the ruling is “public acknowledgment in a court of law and in the top court in the world that what happened to them was genocide,” says O’Brien, who has published multiple books on genocide and international criminal law, is working on a book about the Genocide Convention in the ICJ.
Members of the Rohingya community also said the ruling is a historic recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group.
“Myanmar denies the existence of the Rohingya,” Sayed Ullah, a community leader at a refugee camp in Bangladesh, told the Associated Press , “but now the court made it clear.”
The court’s finding of genocide by a state is a historic first. Two previous genocide cases brought before the ICJ have gone to the merit stages, both arising from the wars that followed the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s.
In 2007, the court ruled on a case brought by Bosnia against Serbia. The court determined that the killing of thousands of Bosniak men and boys in Srebrenica in 1995 was genocide, but it found insufficient evidence to attribute the killings by Bosnian Serb forces to Serbia. Still, the court ruled that Serbia violated its obligation under the Genocide Convention by failing to use its influence over those forces to prevent genocide.
In the second case, which was brought by Croatia against Serbia, the court made no finding that genocide was committed. It instead ruled in a 2015 judgment that Yugoslav army and Serb forces had an intent to ethnically cleanse Croats from Serb-held areas of Croatia, forcing between 80,000 and 100,000 Croats and other non-Serbs to flee the Krajina region between April 1991 and April 1992.
“The Court has not rewritten or expanded the legal definition of genocide” since the earlier cases, Marko Milanovic, a professor of public international law at the University of Reading, said in a statement . “What it has done is take a more flexible approach to the evidence used to establish genocide, particularly the notoriously difficult question of proving genocidal intent.”
The dissenting judges argued that the evidence could support the intent of forced expulsion or collective punishment instead of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group.
The court ordered Myanmar’s military-backed government to ensure the safe, voluntary return of the Rohingya to the country and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.
Myanmar has two years to report to the ICJ on its orders of restitution. If it is unable to carry out restitution, the court ordered the government to pay reparations to the Rohingya, the amount of which will be determined at a later stage.
It’s uncertain whether Myanmar will implement the ruling, which is legally binding.
“Therein lies the rub in that there isn’t necessarily a mechanism for enforcing them,” says O’Brien. If Myanmar does not comply, The Gambia, which brought the case to the ICJ, can turn to the United Nations Security Council, which has discretion over whether to act, although China, which has veto power as a member of the council, is friendly to the Myanmar government.
Third party states can also exert pressure on Myanmar to comply with the ruling, such as through direct diplomatic pressure or sanctions on individuals or companies linked to the genocide. On Thursday, the U.K. ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defense attaché and called for an urgent U.N. Security Council meeting to discuss the judgment. ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights (APHR), an independent group of current and former Southeast Asian parliamentarians, called on the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to support implementation of the ruling. Cheah Wui Ling, an associate professor at the National University of Singapore’s faculty of law, says ASEAN is obligated to “act in ways that respect and not undermine” the ruling, given the organization’s commitment to international law.
Cheah says the ruling could give “fresh momentum” to efforts seeking to hold individuals criminally accountable for the genocide, including an investigation in Argentina and a criminal complaint in Indonesia .
The prosecutor at the International Criminal Court also requested an arrest warrant in 2024 for Min Aung Hlaing. The ruling could have a “snowball effect” on that investigation, says Vincent-Joël Proulx, an associate professor at National University of Singapore’s faculty of law and a former special adviser to the ICJ’s president.
Even so, other challenges remain to seeing restitution through, O’Brien says.
Nine years after the mass displacement, more than a million Rohingya refugees live in Bangladesh, with most in camps in Cox’s Bazar. Some refugees told the AP that they want to return home to Myanmar.
Read More: ‘There Is No Hope’: Death and Desperation Take Over the World’s Largest Refugee Camp
Rohingya refugees visit a market at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 17, 2026. Salahuddin Ahmed—AFP/Getty Images
But many of those homes and villages were completely destroyed, O’Brien says. “They have nothing physically to come back to.” She adds that the Rohingya have faced “decades of discrimination and persecution,” and it’s “very difficult to suddenly turn around a culture of hostility and discrimination.”
Restitution is “trying to put the victims in the position that they were in before this had happened,” says O’Brien. But “so many of them have lost family members, and so many of them have been subject to horrific violence and abuse, so they can’t be put in exactly the same position.”
Eyes are now on South Africa’s genocide case against Israel. The case is in a second round of written pleadings and is expected to take at least three more years.
Myanmar’s defense argued that its military operations targeted militants, not civilians. But the court considered a broader “pattern of conduct” by Myanmar, including hate speech, discriminatory laws, displacement, destruction of property, and widespread sexual violence.

articles.title_orig: Type 004: China’s Fourth Carrier May Outgrow the Ford Class
articles.title_zh: Type 004: China’s Fourth Carrier May Outgrow the Ford Class
articles.content_orig:
by Fortuné Leroy | Nov 21, 2026 | Militärische Luftfahrt , Nachricht | 0 comments
In a dry dock at Dalian, the same one that built China’s first two aircraft carriers, a hull is growing that may end up as long as America’s newest supercarriers. Satellite images taken on 4 September 2026 show the bulbous bow taking shape. Once it is finished, Janes estimates, the ship will be 336 to 339 metres long, marginally longer than USS Gerald R. Ford. Beijing has not given the carrier a name, released a single figure or even confirmed what it is.
Analysts call it the Type 004. It will be China’s fourth carrier, and the first that looks built to match America’s supercarriers rather than chase them.
The work has been visible from orbit since early 2025, when prefabricated modules appeared at Dalian. Keel blocks followed in mid-2025, and by May 2026 imagery showed something no Chinese carrier had had before: two internal compartments, each about 15 by 15 metres, the size and layout analysts would expect for a pair of reactors. The Center for Strategic and International Studies, which has tracked the hull month by month, measured it at about 322 metres from the unfinished bow to the stern in October, with a beam of about 46 metres.
Nuclear power would give the PLA Navy a carrier that can stay at sea for long periods without refuelling and generate the electricity needed for electromagnetic catapults. CSIS rates nuclear propulsion as likely, but it has never been confirmed, and the only other evidence is a land-based prototype naval reactor in Sichuan reported by the Associated Press in 2024.
China’s first two carriers, Liaoning and Shandong, launch their J-15 fighters off a ski-jump bow, which limits how heavy the aircraft can be. Fujian, commissioned at Sanya on 5 November 2025 with Xi Jinping in attendance, was the leap: about 80,000 tonnes, conventionally powered, with three electromagnetic catapults, the technology the US Navy introduced with the Ford in 2017. Her air wing includes the catapult-launched J-15T, the stealthy J-35 and the KJ-600 early-warning aircraft.
Fujian one year after commissioning. Video: CCTV Video News Agency.
The Type 004 is expected to go further. Analysts expect electromagnetic catapults again, possibly four, and a bigger air wing; Lyle Goldstein of Defense Priorities has estimated 75 to 90 aircraft, against roughly 50 to 60 on Fujian. China is also experimenting with drones at sea: in November 2026 the new amphibious assault ship Sichuan launched and recovered a GJ-21 stealth drone with its own electromagnetic catapult.
The United States still operates 11 nuclear-powered carriers, and the second Ford-class ship, John F. Kennedy, reached preliminary acceptance in September 2026, with full delivery due in March 2027. Its first F-35C landing came on 13 October. But the Pentagon’s latest report on China’s military expects the gap in numbers to keep narrowing.
In Washington, meanwhile, the argument is about going backwards. An August White House memo ordered a plan to fit the future USS Doris Miller with steam catapults instead of electromagnetic ones. On 17 November 2026, Senator Roger Wicker, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, told the Navy’s leadership in a hearing that “returning to steam is a non-starter, and everybody needs to understand that.”
Flight operations aboard USS Gerald R. Ford. Video: US Navy.
Almost everything about the Type 004 is still an estimate: its final length, its displacement, its power plant and the number of catapults. China has confirmed none of it. If it follows Fujian’s pattern, the hull could float out of the dock in 2027, and the carrier could join the fleet some years after that. What the satellites already make clear is the ambition: a Chinese carrier built in the same weight class as the American ones.

Ford command history; Associated Press (2024).

articles.title_orig: Two tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as hawks press Trump to resume Iran strikes
articles.title_zh: Two tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as hawks press Trump to resume Iran strikes
articles.content_orig:
Two tankers were reportedly struck by projectiles near the Strait of Hormuz Saturday, raising fears of a new escalation in the crucial oil-shipping corridor as Israel and administration hawks press President Trump to renew major attacks on Iran.
One tanker attempting to leave the strait was struck in the stern, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency, while a second reported a projectile hitting its engine room. No casualties were reported.
Trump is facing calls from inside and outside his administration to resume major attacks on Iran that have been on pause since the summer, despite repeated strikes and counter strikes in the region.
Israel’s ambassador to the US, Michael Leiter, told The Post this week that his country “believes ousting the Tehran regime is now the only long- or even medium-term answer,” adding that Israel “will not hesitate to go it alone” because the situation is “existential.”
Leiter also faced backlash after telling Newsmax: “You get American soldiers back here to the United States, to their families, when Iran is defeated.”
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi mocked the remarks on X. “We did not know that the Israeli Ambassador to Washington was the commander-in-chief of the U.S. Military,” he wrote.
Amid the backlash, Leiter sought to make clear that he was not suggesting Israel could dictate US military policy.
“Let’s state the obvious: only the President of the United States decides when and where American troops are deployed,” he wrote on X.
Hawks within the US administration are pushing to resume strikes as well, Britain’s Financial Times reported.
US Central Command has reportedly warned officials about the strain a prolonged military buildup is placing on American forces, even as congressional Democrats prepare to challenge funding for the campaign.
“Centcom is telling the administration that they’re running out of time, burning money and readiness,” a source told the paper. A US official disputed that characterization.
President Trump on Friday accused Iran of refusing to negotiate a deal acceptable to Washington.
“They want to make a deal, but they don’t want to make a deal that’s acceptable to me. We want to make a real deal, not a real deal that they’ve been doing for 51 years,” he told reporters.
“They’ve been bull——g people for 51 years,” he added.
Trump repeated his vow that “Iran will never have a nuclear weapon ever,” but his administration faces a potential congressional battle over the cost of the conflict as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers.
Iran, meanwhile, appears to be preparing a challenge to the US naval blockade.
More than a dozen Iranian oil tankers have reportedly gathered near Kharg Island, the country’s principal oil-export terminal, as Tehran weighs ways to move crude despite the blockade, Defense News reported.
Iran’s state-affiliated Fars News Agency has floated the idea of a tanker convoy through the Gulf of Oman to get Iranian oil to market.
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
The US has launched repeated strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island this month , while Iran has continued to lob attacks at US allies, including targeting drone and missile strikes at Kuwait .
On the nuclear front, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran had not changed its official position on nuclear weapons despite international pressure and debate over its nuclear doctrine.
China and Russia oppose any change in Tehran’s nuclear doctrine, Araghchi said, according to Iran Daily.
“What matters is that, up to this point, our doctrine has not changed, and our official positions remain the same as before,” Araghchi said.
Iran is a signatory to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, but its nuclear program has long drawn international scrutiny over undeclared activities, underground facilities and restrictions on UN inspections. Washington has accused Tehran of seeking the capability to build nuclear weapons.

articles.title_orig: A 10% drop for the stock market is unnerving, but it’s not that unusual
articles.title_zh: A 10% drop for the stock market is unnerving, but it’s not that unusual
articles.content_orig:
As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off , prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year.
On platform Kalshi , speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%.
Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices.
On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, primarily those with exposure to the artificial intelligence build-out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory, too.
The S&P 500 has slashed its year-to-date gain to just over 2%.
The Stock Trader's Almanac in a Thursday note broadly agreed that the hopes for a December rally are fading, with the caveat that a "Santa rally" could still appear at the end of the year.
"The market is under pressure and more downside can't be ruled out," the note said.
The Stock Trader's Almanac sees 2026 following the year-end pattern of 2018, when the Federal Reserve was in a tightening cycle in a midterm year. The Fed is widely expected to hike rates at its December meeting.
In that scenario, the Stock Trader's Almanac thinks more churn is to come. "The low is more likely in mid- to late December than this week."

articles.title_orig: Cargo ship bound for Russia's Kaliningrad hit by drones, Finland tightens security
articles.title_zh: Cargo ship bound for Russia's Kaliningrad hit by drones, Finland tightens security
articles.content_orig:
The crew of a Russian ship in the Gulf of Finland, hit by drones likely launched by Ukraine, is being evacuated into life rafts and a rescue boat.
Finnish authorities say the Sparta II has links to Russia’s armed forces and has drifted into territorial waters off Finland’s southern coast.
“There is a fire on board the ship. The situation does not pose a danger to maritime traffic or people. A restricted area has been set up around the site to ensure safety,” the Finnish Border Guard said in a statement, adding that it is in “close international cooperation” with neighbouring countries, including contact with Russia’s maritime rescue authorities.
On Saturday morning, Finland’s Ministry of Defence said its forces detected a drone attack on a Russian vessel in international waters, with initial reports saying the ship had sustained damage. Finnish Border Guard units were dispatched to the scene, and a photograph taken by a Finnish patrol plane showed flames and thick smoke coming from the rear of the ship.
The attack happened west of Gogland Island, off the coast of the Finnish town of Loviisa, and Finland quickly implemented temporary air and sea traffic restrictions in the eastern part of the gulf.
A Russian helicopter has since violated Finnish airspace, venturing more than 4km into Finnish territory.
“The suspected airspace violation is possibly related to rescue or tracking operations of a damaged cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland. The Defence Forces and the Border Guard are handling the situation in cooperation with other authorities,” said Minister of Defence Antti Hakkanen.
By Saturday afternoon the Finnish Defence Forces said the strike was likely carried out by Ukraine. Earlier, Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo wrote on X that “war is spilling over into our immediate vicinity. The Finnish authorities are handling the situation in the Gulf of Finland, where a drone strike has hit a Russian merchant vessel. Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”
Finland’s Border Guard said the Sparta II is known to have links to Russia’s armed forces. The roll-on-roll-off ship was built in the year 2000 and sails under a Russian flag, according to the vesselfinder.com website.
“At the moment, ⁠⁠⁠⁠there is no confirmed information about ⁠⁠⁠⁠what cargo is on ⁠⁠⁠⁠board, but ⁠⁠⁠⁠it cannot be ruled out that there ‌‌‌‌is military materiel on board,” Iljin said.
Alexander Drozdenko, governor of Russia’s Leningrad region, said damage to the ship had yet to be fully assessed.
“Three nautical miles from the Russian Federation’s border, a cargo vessel bound for Kaliningrad was attacked by two drones,” he wrote on the messaging app Max.
Kaliningrad’s Governor Alexey Besprozvannykh said supplies to the Russian exclave were not at risk.
One of the major risks of attacking any vessel is environmental damage if it leaks or sinks, a scenario that Baltic Sea nations treat with high importance. That risk is “further amplified by the poor state of some of the so-called ‘Shadow Fleet’ tankers” that Russia operates, according to Robin Haggblom, senior adviser for Risk Intelligence and an expert in Finnish maritime issues.
“Actions to prevent environmental damage has also been emphasised in Finnish Border Guard communication regarding this event. Luckily in this case, we don’t yet have ice coverage in the Gulf of Finland, which would impact any oil spill recovery efforts that may be needed,” Haggblom told Al Jazeera.
The narrow and shallow waters of the Baltic Sea are some of the most crowded shipping lanes in the world. The Helsinki to Tallinn ferry route had 7.5m passenger crossings last year. Other passenger routes link Baltic ports and capital cities, and cargo vessels and military shipping contribute to the total number of vessels in the relatively small body of water.
So if Ukraine is using drones – maritime or aerial – to hit Russian ships, could there be any risks to civilian vessels?
“There obviously always is a risk of collateral damage. However, so far Ukraine does seem to be taking a number of steps to minimise the risks involved, with the Sparta II for example apparently having been identified and hit a handful of kilometres from Russian waters,” added expert Haggblom.
Earlier this month, Finland’s military said it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland, which Ukraine took credit for. Helsinki later said it had raised concerns with Kyiv about strikes in the area.
“It is the same with the strike on the Russian corvette earlier, where it is reported the Ukrainians were able to pick it out and target that specific vessel among perhaps a dozen other ships. There are also unconfirmed indications that Sparta II was targeted specifically, and not just as a general Russia-associated merchant vessel,” Häggblom added.
Ukraine and Russia have attacked each other’s shipping throughout the war, mostly in the Black Sea.

articles.title_orig: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.title_zh: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.
This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.
Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.
A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".
Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".
Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.
"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."
Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."
In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".
The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.
It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.
Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

articles.title_orig: International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
articles.title_zh: International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
articles.content_orig:
A Ukrainian FP-1 long-range attack drone is launched at an undisclosed location in Ukraine, Aug. 16, 2026. Efrem Lukatsky/AP hide caption
GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."
After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.
Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.
Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo .
Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan , 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.
Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.
"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."
No one went into the negotiations thinking they would be easy; some of the world's most powerful countries, among them the U.S., Russia and Israel, had already indicated their reluctance to agree to binding regulations.
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting's agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.
"They're just kicking the can down the road," said one frustrated delegate. As the clock ticked on and the weekend approached, diplomats scrambled to get some kind of result from negotiations that had been billed as a last chance to regulate weapons whose technology and decision-making capabilities we may not even fully understand.
Finally, at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday morning, they emerged from the negotiating room to announce their compromise: no to a deal within a year, maybe to legally binding rules, or maybe not.
The ICRC immediately said it regretted the move and renewed its appeal for a binding treaty. Other campaigners were less polite, calling the deal "a real disappointment" and a "nothing burger." "I am concerned people will die because of this," added another.
A key worry is that, with two years to talk about possible rules that might only be optional, the technology will race ahead, uncontrolled.
"We're likely to see the systems proliferate," said Anna Hehir, an expert in military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute. "They're not like nuclear weapons in that they're inaccessible. There are autonomous weapons that are easy to purchase or even to create for all kinds of actors: individuals, nonstate actors, criminal groups."
There are also big questions about how our existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – can be upheld if those doing the killing are not humans, but machines.
"These rules are the bare minimum that militaries and states have developed and agreed to adhere to," said the ICRC's Hinds. "The commander remains responsible for making sure that the use of force is lawful. The commander remains accountable. You cannot hold a machine accountable for a violation of the law."
But in the race to develop new weapons, no country wants to come second. Although most U.N. member states do agree there should be some controls over autonomous weapons, the compromise in Geneva means that, for the next two years at least, weapons that can use artificial intelligence to make life-and-death decisions will remain unregulated.
Meanwhile, weapons technology is developing at pace, while diplomacy is struggling to keep up.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street Asks What Can Save AI Trade After Anthropic Wipeout
articles.title_zh: Wall Street Asks What Can Save AI Trade After Anthropic Wipeout
articles.content_orig:
Stocks got hit hard this week amid fears that the AI trade could be buckling. Spencer Platt/Getty Images hide caption
A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion.
AI-related stocks have powered markets to record highs and helped support the broader economy. But investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions.
Here's what to know about the week in AI and why alarm bells are ringing
Investors were hoping the stock market debut of AI giant Anthropic this week would provide a boost to the markets. Instead, the entire stock market got pummeled on Friday, sparking one of the worst weeks that Wall Street has seen in quite some time.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 10% for the week, its worst performance since the onset of COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns in March 2020. Even Anthropic, which gained 17% on its debut, ended up slumping more than 8% to close near its IPO price on Friday.
Meanwhile, both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average entered a correction as of the close of trade on Friday, meaning a drop of 10% from their recent highs.
It's the culmination of weeks of fears that have been building up about the sustainability of the AI trade.
Back in September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years. That poses a big challenge to AI companies because they still need to borrow billions of dollars to do things like build out data centers that power the growth of their technologies. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for them.
Democrats also took over both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, vowing to take a tougher regulatory approach toward the AI sector and slow down the build-out of data centers, which have been unpopular with voters .
Democrats were also elected as governors in states that have been key to the data center build-out, like Texas, where Gina Hinojosa stunned the political world by winning her race .
And then there's the turmoil at Nvidia, the top AI chip company. Its CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned this month after being suspected of having had an affair with a woman who's believed to have been spying for China.
All this has exacerbated investors' worries about the sustainability of an AI trade into which investors have sunk billions of dollars.
Hank Smith, the head of investment strategy at Haverford Trust, thinks it's unlikely the markets will recover quickly, the way they have previously bounced right back after AI shares dropped.
"I think it has taken the market the better part of the last two or three weeks to realize it is not going to be like the previous sell-offs," Smith said, adding that AI could fall "out of favor" through next year.
"It's just going to take a little bit of time to heal," he said of the tech market.
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO this month, throwing the company's leadership into turmoil. Here, Huang delivers a keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas on Jan. 6, 2025. Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
That has been a big source of debate on Wall Street.
Some people fear that the AI sector could be in the middle of a bubble that is bursting, just like tech stocks did during the dot-com bust of 2000. At the time, investors had sunk money into tech companies that often had no profits — and not even revenues — and were wiped out in the bust.
Smith, though, argues that this time around the AI trade is being powered by top companies such as Meta and Apple, and he doesn't see them as likely to go out of business, the way many dot-coms did. Nvidia — despite its leadership shake-up — still posted strong results this week.
The future prospects for AI, Smith said, are "not based on a pie in the sky."
That said, Smith continued, there is still a question about whether investors will see the sizable returns they are hoping to get.
And there's another big fear: how interconnected AI companies have become. Nvidia, for example, not only owns shares in other big AI companies like Anthropic but is also lending a lot of money to them. In turn, they are buying chips from Nvidia.
This circular system of financing also involves lesser-known companies, such as CoreWeave, that are borrowing heavily to build out data centers. Nvidia is a major investor in CoreWeave, in another sign of the interconnectedness .
This close-knit ecosystem is raising concerns that if one or two companies run into trouble, it could kick off a chain reaction that could lead to something like a financial crisis.
It could be potentially significant. The U.S. economy has effectively become an AI economy.
Building out data centers, for example, may be unpopular with voters, but construction creates jobs, which is why some parts of the U.S. have courted the centers. In fact, AI investments helped the economy grow at an annual rate of 3.4% in the most recent quarter.
Not only that, but AI-related stocks have become an integral part of the broader markets, accounting for a substantial portion of the S&P 500. That means many investors hold these stocks as part of their portfolios, including as components of index funds, pensions or retirement funds like 401(k)s.
So if the AI trade unravels, it could have a ripple effect far beyond the high-tech world.

articles.title_zh: The Outages Are Just Getting Started
articles.content_orig:
Welcome to Kernel Panic , a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here .
Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks , United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.
So let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.
AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs . Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to quickly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.
Microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed update in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials said this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates . Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”
External pressures and bugs in patches are not new, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.
“Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” says Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.”
IT administrators are leaning on AI more as well to accelerate their evaluation and prepare their systems for updates, but current AI tools still can’t replace human analysis and planning.
“AI can help, but people still need to understand what went wrong, check that the patch addresses the cause, and look for similar issues elsewhere,” says Lea Schönherr, a tenure-track faculty member at CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, a German national research institution. “Rolling out patches across widely used systems also takes time.”
Matthew Prince, CEO and cofounder of the web infrastructure giant Cloudflare, predicts that “it’s going to feel like the sky is falling for two years.” He suspects, though, that eventually AI acceleration will help defenders get on top of common vulnerabilities and better secure software in general. “These new threats and new security vulnerabilities won’t happen as often, and the background noise will actually tick down quite a bit,” he predicts.
Still, the evidence that AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity is mounting. This week the total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 surpassed 100,000 . To put that into perspective, in 2022, the final year before LLMs went mainstream, there were around 25,000 recorded vulnerabilities. And this year’s figure, with more than a month still to go, is double the combined totals of 2024 and 2025.
In the last few days, researchers disclosed that they used AI to find critical vulnerabilities in PHP (for the second time), open source web server software NGINX, and programming language Java. Forbes also reported on 35 vulnerabilities across iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple Watches, and other products from the company that had been discovered by researchers using AI.
There are important nuances to consider, though. Not all AI-discovered vulnerabilities are ultimately that impactful. “The number of vulnerabilities has certainly exploded, but the number of vulnerabilities that you need to care about has remained somewhat constant,” Slowik says. “The caveat is that the pace at which they’re being used or weaponized has increased dramatically.”
Only 300 vulnerabilities have been added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of exploited vulnerabilities this year—meaning the flaws that hackers successfully used to their advantage is far lower than the total number of discovered bugs. VulnCheck, which runs its own database, puts the number of known exploited vulnerabilities higher , at 1,500 so far in 2026, which is still just 1.5 percent of the total number of bugs discovered this year.
“What matters to me is that we avoid blaming AI when things go wrong,” says Schönherr, the German researcher. “Responsibility lies with the people and companies that choose to use AI and give it access to infrastructure, and there should be consequences and regulations that can be applied.”
Additional reporting by Andy Greenberg.
• Double take. After being impacted in the outages earlier this week, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that hackers have, in a separate incident, stolen some company data. The bank says “attackers accessed certain marketing data” that was held by third parties it works with. This “may” include customer information such as names and emails, JPMorgan Chase said in a statement reported by Reuters . The security incidents are not linked to any of the outages, though, the company said. Visa and Mastercard also had data impacted in attacks against their vendors.
• Police in the Netherlands revealed that they’ve thwarted several “attempts at violence” directed toward customers of the digital bank Revolut. In September the fintech company was reportedly compromised, with customer data being stolen. The National Police Corps published a statement saying they had made several arrests “which can be linked to the data theft.” It’s unclear who was being targeted, but over the last few years there has been an increase in physical attacks (sometimes known as “ wrench attacks ”) against wealthy cryptocurrency holders, who are forced to hand over money while being held hostage .
• Confirm and deny. The UK government has been forced by a court ruling to admit that it ordered Apple to circumvent its own encryption and access customer iCloud data. British officials had maintained it would damage national security to confirm that it had issued Apple a “technical capability notice” last year—under British laws, the notices are supposed to be shrouded in secrecy and not talked about in public. However, as Computer Weekly reports , the existence of the order was widely known, with top Trump officials publicly criticizing it and even UK government officials allegedly briefing newspapers about the order.

The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again.
That vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship 's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX 's Starbase site in South Texas.
Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk , who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen.
"In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk said on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit .
He didn't say where Ship would be put on display, but the likeliest locale is Starbase, SpaceX's Starship manufacturing and launch hub. (SpaceX plans to shift most Starship launches to its new Starbase Louisiana site, but construction has yet to begin on that $100 billion complex.)
Musk participated virtually in the TomorrowX conversation, which was moderated by two friends of his, the venture capitalists Gavin Baker and Antonio Gracias. (TomorrowX took place in Austin, Texas, but Musk was in China on Wednesday as part of President Trump's delegation for his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.)
The world's richest man expounded on Ship 42's historic achievement, explaining that it gets SpaceX much closer to the "holy grail of rocketry" — a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle.
Before Flight 15, SpaceX had already caught Starship's first-stage booster, known as Super Heavy, on three separate occasions , and it had reflown a booster twice. But the company had never attempted a Ship catch, which is a taller order, given how much faster and farther Starship upper stages fly.
So snagging Ship on the first try was a very big deal, according to Musk.
"Everyone knew, within SpaceX, at least, how important this milestone was, and that it was really something fundamental and profound — that Starship will be the first-ever fully reusable orbital space system," he told Baker and Gracias on Wednesday.
And SpaceX is very serious about Starship reuse. Musk has said that the company wants to launch about 10,000 Starship missions per year by 2030.
This mind-boggling cadence will help the company build out two enormous megaconstellations in low Earth orbit — the next iteration of its Starlink broadband network, which will consist of about 100,000 satellites , and its Starmind AI data-center constellation, which will be 10 times bigger than that .
Assembly of that new Starlink network is already underway. Ship carried 26 of the next-gen internet spacecraft up for the first time on Flight 14 , which launched on Sept. 28, and repeated the feat on Flight 15.
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. articles.title_orig: My Mother-in-Law Only Wants to Talk About One Creepy Thing at Family Gatherings. I Can’t Take Another Minute.
articles.title_zh: My Mother-in-Law Only Wants to Talk About One Creepy Thing at Family Gatherings. I Can’t Take Another Minute.
articles.content_orig:

Dear Prudence is Slate’s advice column. Submit questions here .
Every time my in-laws come over for a holiday meal or we go to their place, my mother-in-law “Gertrude” will launch into how her husband “Paul,” and her favorite line of attack has crossed the line.
All she wants to talk about is how he has failed to satisfy her sexually over the course of their marriage. Most of the other relatives will giggle and make crude comments to Paul as he is forced to sit there stewing in silence while his drunken wife turns him into a laughing stock. I have always found Gertrude’s behavior extremely off-putting. When I asked my husband to speak to his mother about it, he said she’s been doing it since he was a kid and won’t change. Should I stick up for my FIL the next time Gertrude starts up, or is it none of my business?
—Pop Is a Proverbial Punching Bag
This fact pattern feels so familiar. I’m sure I’ve answered similar letters, in which an older woman is sharing her bedroom complaints with her husband over a family meal—at least three times. I don’t know what to make of the fact that senior sexual shaming at the dinner table seems to be an epidemic, but your story includes the upsetting addition of relatives treating the inappropriate rants as a comedy routine, which makes things even worse.
You probably won’t be able to put an end to a longstanding disturbing family tradition. I’m not even sure that it’s appropriate for you to stand up for Paul. Who knows, maybe he’s been a lazy, selfish partner who doesn’t consider any of Gertrude’s needs, sexual or other, and ranting about him at Thanksgiving is the one way she evens the score. There could be more to the story. Or she could just be really mean. But you probably don’t want to get too involved in trying to manage their relationship. Instead, limit your comments to the part that is your business: You don’t want to hear about this! But you should say something.
“Whoa, this is really TMI.”
“Do you mind not talking about this while we eat?”
“I’m not comfortable with this conversation.”
“Hey Gertrude, we’ve heard this before. Does anyone want to talk about anything new going on in their life?”

I have a very competent and dedicated assistant who fills her professional role beautifully. The issue is that it is not the only thing that she fills beautifully. She’s a former ballet dancer, is extremely fit, and by any objective standard is hotter than a solar flare. I feel like I am flying too close to the sun. Quite apart from the fact that she’s my assistant, we are both attached, she’s far too young for me and she is most certainly not my type—any romantic attachment is completely out of the question. On the physical appearance side, I’ve had to tell other men in the coworking building to knock it off when they talk about her. Personally, with her, I steer well clear of any discussions of how she looks or dresses, etc. However, she almost always wears a strong and intoxicating perfume and she will show up in the office in very short cocktail-like dresses that really accentuate her outstanding physique, or attire that exposes a deep cleavage—I would not say that what she wears is unprofessional by today’s standards—but I am secretly crying out for mercy inside while I try my best to keep my head down and focused on work.
Her desk is right next to mine in a cozy open plan office that is usually empty except us because most employees either work from home or do technical work in specialist labs, so I spend many long hours alone with her. It’s a small company that I run and there is no HR and no other role for her—not that those would be “solutions.” My feelings are not romantic, lustful maybe and they get stronger with every vaguely flirtatious flick of her hair, glance, or laugh from a not particularly funny statement of mine. I worry that if I continue to sit next to this bubbling caldera that the fire of those desires may destroy everything—It would only take a few misplaced words uttered in a moment of weakness. It ain’t the volcano’s fault if I sit too close and turn myself into a cinder. But moving away seems problematic also. What should I do?
The key here is a mindset shift. You have to try to get as excited about being a non-creepy man as you currently are about this beautiful woman’s appearance. Being professional, maintaining a good reputation, and contributing to a working relationship in which your assistant can thrive without fending off advances or weird vibes are all things you can succeed at legitimately be proud of. Maybe read some perspectives of young women about how annoying and gross some of the treatment they receive in the workplace is. Explore the idea that when she’s laughing at your jokes or smiling at you, those are simply attempts at being kind and pleasant in a way that is often expected of women, especially. Then, get fired up about living a life in which you are never going to be the lecherous boss in someone’s horror story. Put all of your energy into this because the other plan isn’t going to end well. She hasn’t and most likely won’t want to date or sleep with you, no matter what you do: The “few misplaced words” that feel tempting to say would not actually open up a romantic relationship with her. It’s more likely that they would send her to her group chat with several vomit emojis.
I grew up in a household where physical affection and even physical contact outside of things like assistance with bathing and dressing when I was a young child was non-existent. I literally can remember the first time I was ever hugged. It was by my kindergarten teacher on the last day of school to say goodbye. The reason I remember is because I completely freaked out and struggled to get away because I didn’t understand what was happening. My poor teacher felt terrible (Mrs. K, if you’re out there, sorry!). I’ve tried to get over it, but even to this day I reflexively stiffen when someone hugs me; if someone even touches me, I flinch. This hurts people’s feelings and I feel badly about it, but for me the reaction is as natural as having a leg jump when the doctor taps your knee with the rubber mallet. The holidays are an especially problematic time for me considering. Obviously, I can’t give a lengthy personal story about my childhood to everyone who gets put off by my reaction. Do you have any advice on how I can become more comfortable with casual physical affection?
—Still Getting Used to Touch
There are probably two parts of this: 1) How to get people to give you space when you don’t want to be touched and 2) How to get more comfortable, which probably isn’t going to happen via self-styled exposure therapy at the door of a holiday party when someone who’s already had two cocktails is bombarding you with a too-tight embrace. So don’t try to force yourself to “get over it” in these situations. Instead, make an announcement in advance. This could happen casually, in offhand remarks to individual friends and family members about how you really prefer not to be touched. You could use social media to repost relatable content in a lighthearted public service announcement to your followers. Or, if you have one main friend group, you might even try a note in the group chat (“Most of you know this about me but because of the way I was raised without a lot of physical contact I’m not very comfortable with hugging and stuff. Since we’ll all be getting together soon, I just wanted to remind everyone so you don’t think it’s personal if I get stiff or flinch. I
