articles.title_orig: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
articles.title_zh: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
articles.content_orig:
Paul Smith, chief commercial officer of Anthropic, center left, and Krishna Rao, chief financial officer of Anthropic, center right, alongside others react during the closing bell ceremony for the Anthropic IPO at Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. Seth Wenig/AP hide caption
A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude.
It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.
Levent Alpöge, a member of the company's technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.
"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."
Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow towards infinity.
Alpöge said his discovery came late Sunday night. He messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about "my ability to announce," as the San Francisco-based company was about to make major news with its stock market debut.
A day after the company's initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he'd solved the problem that has proved elusive for more than 150 years. Anthropic did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on Alpöge's claim.
Alpöge released his and Claude's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis within 17 million lines of Lean code, a programing language that allows people to program proofs of mathematical theorems. Traditionally the findings buried in that code would be published in a formal paper, said Alex Kontorovich, distinguished professor and department chair of mathematics at Rutgers University.
"Usually when somebody gives you a paper, that's also kind of code for a proof and you have to actually read the paper, follow it yourself, figure out if you believe every single line in that paper. And when you're done, you should have a deep understanding of why something is true," he said.
He said Claude followed that code and said the proof is true.
"Does that mean I understand it? Not yet. But the computer is extraordinarily picky, way pickier than I am and so if you can satisfy the computer, there's a very, very good chance you're going to satisfy me too," he said. "But I have to do the work."
Hours after the announcement, the Riemann Hypothesis remained listed as unsolved on the Clay Mathematics Institute's website. The institute had selected the hypothesis back in 2000 as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems and offered a reward of $1 million for the solution.
The assessment process of whether the problem has actually been solved takes time, explained Martin Bridson, president of the institute.
"This is an announcement of historic significance, which holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics," he said in a statement. "But the journey from today's announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult."
Alpöge said he is "presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics." He said more than 250,000 pages came out of his work with AI.
In September, OpenAI said its technology was key in a similar breakthrough with Navier-Stokes, an equation that governs the flow of fluids.
"Navier-Stokes fell and now the Riemann Hypothesis," said Kontorovich. "There's some kind of out-of-body experience where I'm looking at myself saying, 'Yes, the Riemann Hypothesis has been solved,' and kind of trying to comprehend what the hell these words are coming out of my mouth."
Anthropic made a blockbuster Wall Street debut this week, through which it raised a record-breaking $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation.
Amodei has projected an optimistic vision for AI's future in which the technology leads to significant advancements in math and science research while simultaneously warning about the potential risks AI poses.

articles.title_orig: South West birdwatchers describe thrill of starling murmations
articles.title_zh: South West birdwatchers describe thrill of starling murmations
articles.content_orig:
Birdwatchers have described their joy at seeing starling murmations as a survey seeks to build a picture of their numbers.
Researchers from the University of Gloucester are updating a survey conducted a decade ago which examined the behaviour of the birds to find out what has changed.
Murmurations are lauded as one of "nature's winter wonders" as they involve masses of starlings swooping and diving in a pattern before roosting.
Encouraging people to participate in the survey, Devon artist Mike Langman said the dances were "just absolutely stunning", while Cornwall photographer Peter Glaser described murmations as "hair-raising".
The study hopes to find out if murmurations happen in the same places, if bird numbers have stayed the same and whether birds of prey are still around.
The 2014-16 study found there was an average of 30,000 birds in a murmuration, while some of the larger ones had more than 750,000 birds, based on sightings from 23 countries.
As part of the original study, researchers backed the idea that murmurations are primarily to protect birds against predators such as peregrine falcons and sparrowhawks.
Langman, who leads guided bird tours, encouraged citizen scientists to join in "for the experience as much as anything else".
He nominated his best spots for murmations in Devon as Countess Wear, near Topsham, and Thurlestone and Slapton Ley in the South Hams.
"Not only do you see them, you hear them as well and sometimes you even smell them," he said.
He said the sounds could be "remarkable" as tens of thousands of birds twist and turn before roosting when they fall silent.
"It's just like someone has switched off a light switch," he said.
Photographer Peter Glaser, who has captured many murmurations at Roughtor on Bodmin Moor, said they were "absolutely enthralling" to see.
He noted numbers this year "seem to be quite a marked improvement" on previous years.
"The expressions of delight [from others], the hairs on the back of your head rising, it is incredible," he said.
Wadebridge-based photographer Adrian Langdon said starlings often gathered at Penzance rail and bus station and Marazion Marsh.
"It's one of the spectacles of the natural world... it's pretty special," he said.
Prof Adam Hart from the University of Gloucester, who is leading the survey, asked people to provide accurate estimates of the number of starlings in the group as well as recording any birds of prey.
"We may see fewer birds, we may see fewer murmurations. We don't really know and that's the point of doing the survey," he said.

articles.title_orig: International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin
articles.title_zh: International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin
articles.content_orig:
The era of U.S. airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed. In its place will be a massive business-class cabin with room for 70 passengers.
U.S. airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a new top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines have already taken this step. American was the last of the U.S. airlines to still have first class on long-haul international routes.
Many travelers might not notice the difference. That's because of airlines' investments into business class: new suites , bigger screens, better technology like device-charging pads, and improved bedding.
It's part of airlines' big bet on mass luxury. Consumers have been willing to shell out more to fly comfortably, which is helping to boost airline revenue. That's all the more important as costs of everything from fuel to airport landing fees have been rising, soaking up more of the industry's profits.
The retirement of first class ends a more-than-six-decade stretch of the jet age that in the early days included service like seat-side carving of chateaubriand and meals served on fine bone china.
A few decades ago, business class was much smaller, with two-by-two seats in some configurations, and recliners, not the lie-flat seats that dominate those cabins now.
"When you've got individual pods in biz class, and you've got a comfortable enough seat and bedding and decent wine, for a lot of people this is good enough," said Henry Harteveldt, founder of travel consulting firm Atmosphere Research Group and a former airline executive.
The over-the-top dining of the early days of international first class was a form of entertainment, long before laptops, personal seat-back screens and in-flight Wi-Fi, or even the promise of sleep on lie-flat beds, but customers still eat lots on board, Harteveldt said.
"People say they want to sleep but then they stay up and they eat every morsel," he said. "They're hypocrites."
There was still a hefty price gap between first and business.
A flight between Los Angeles and London on American's Boeing 777-300ER this week went for $12,994 in business class for a one-way ticket and $15,669 for a first-class seat.
American's last flight with international first class departed Friday morning local time in Sydney, bound for Los Angeles.
Its new cabin on its Boeing 777-300ERs will feature 70 business-class suites, the most of any U.S. airline. Pre-overhaul, the cabins had been operating with eight first-class suites and 52 pods in business, though the remodeling is ongoing. American is also flying a subfleet of 787-9 Dreamliners that have 51 business-class suites. (United is putting 64 new suites on that aircraft.)
Part of the allure is that some companies allow employees to book business-class tickets, but not first class.
American Airlines told CNBC it's growing its business-class cabins across the fleet. It's evaluating increasing the number of suites on its smaller long-haul jets, the Boeing 787-8 Dreamliners, from 20 currently to somewhere in the 30s.
"You don't have enough seats to make the seat cost competitive," Nat Pieper, American's chief commercial officer, said in an interview this month. "So what you need to do to make that airplane work is it's got to be a yield play. You need more business-class seats."
Differences between first and business classes on American lately came down to details.
On American's first-class long-haul section, passengers got olives with warm nuts to accompany their beverage early in the flight, while there were no olives for business class.
First class got a soup; business did not. First class got a warm dessert served a la mode in addition to the cold dessert or fruit and cheese plate both cabins were offered.
And there was no memory foam lumbar pillow for business class like there was in first, American said. But otherwise, the experiences were fairly similar for passengers. They still got better food options and service than economy passengers, along with their bigger seats, early boarding and lounge access.
"It's not like the bed can go any flatter than 180 degrees," Harteveldt said. "The bedding can be thicker, and the food nicer."
Delta and United have already replaced international, long-haul first class with dozens of their Delta One and Polaris business lie-flat suites , respectively, each of which is getting upgrades now.
American will continue offering a separate lie-flat first class on its Airbus A321T subfleet it uses for domestic cross-country flying until early 2027. But then that goes away, too.
Meanwhile, airlines over the past decade have added a premium economy section, which sits between business class and economy. It features recliner seats similar to those in domestic first class, often with foot rests, meals served on actual plates, larger seat-back screens than economy and earlier boarding.
Airlines are now cutting up business class into different segments, something they've done for more than a decade with the coach cabin's basic economy, standard and extra legroom seats.
United and Delta this year each announced their most expensive cabins will be sold with basic options , which are more restrictive and don't include things like the ability to pick your seat ahead of time or get access to a special airport lounge.
There are also a few seats in some of the business-class cabins that are roomier, like American's Flagship Suite Preferred and United's Polaris Studio. Even the guest seating in the United suite varies with "standard and companion ottomans," the latter including a seatbelt so you can ask "another Polaris passenger to visit you between takeoff and landing for a drink, chat or game," the airline says.
"I don't think we found the limit on segmentation," United CFO Mike Leskinen told CNBC on Thursday. "We have a few things on the drawing board. We're not done."
Although U.S. carriers are moving away from the designation, first class is far from dead.
Singapore Airlines, Germany's Lufthansa, British Airways and Air France have unveiled updated first-class cabins and other service improvements like food.
British Airways last month said it will build a record 106-suite business class on its Airbus A380 aircraft, the world's largest passenger airplane, but it's also upgrading its first class on board.
Meanwhile, smaller airlines like JetBlue Airways , Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air are introducing domestic or short-haul first-class seats .
"We're going to be able to do that at a really low price comparatively to what you're used to out there in the marketplace," Frontier Chief Commercial Officer Bobby Schroeter said last month.

articles.title_orig: Costa revives EU digital tax proposal in bid to reach agreement on budget
articles.title_zh: Costa revives EU digital tax proposal in bid to reach agreement on budget
articles.content_orig:
The EU has put forward plans to tax the world's biggest digital companies to fund its next budget, as it seeks to bridge divisions among member states over the bloc's long-term funding.
European Council President António Costa unveiled a new spending proposal that cuts by €204 billion a plan initially put forward by the European Commission, which some countries had criticised as too onerous.
"I believe this proposal can bring us closer to a final agreement," Mr Costa told a press conference in Brussels.
EU countries have been squabbling over the size of the next budget, with Germany leading calls for major cuts after the commission last year proposed a two-trillion-euro budget for the 2028 - 2034 period.
Berlin criticised a revised proposal published last month that suggested slashing the bloc's future seven-year budget by €140 billion.
Mr Costa, who represents the EU's 27 states, is seeking to reach a deal by the end of the year balancing contributions from member states with new sources of revenue for the bloc.
Among these could be a tax on digital firms that the draft Mr Costa presented today says will concern companies with an annual turnover for digital activities of at least €50 million in the EU as well as a global turnover of more than €750 million.
They would be subjected to "an annual contribution corresponding to 3% of the annual net turnover from online advertising, digital intermediation services and user-generated data", according to documents shared by the council.
The plan is likely to provoke criticism from US President Donald Trump.
His administration has reacted angrily to EU fines and moves against big tech under its content and competition rules in recent years.
The draft also includes plans for a levy on electronic waste and higher tobacco taxes.
The document will be at the centre of hours of fraught talks when EU leaders meet in Brussels next week.
Mr Costa is pushing for a deal in December amid EU fears that a delay would push talks into a fraught election year in 2027, with worries about what potential eurosceptic victories in France and elsewhere would mean for future dealmaking.
Once EU states find an agreement, they will have to negotiate with parliament - a task that also promises to be difficult.
Key budget politician Siegfried Mureșan warned the EU Parliament would block the spending plan if member states continued to ignore its concerns.
"We think that the debate ... is focused too much on cuts," he said this week.
Germany is part of a grouping with five other so-called "frugal" EU members, including Sweden, which expressed scepticism this week over new taxes.
"It's money taken from somewhere else. It won't solve the financial equation," Swedish Europe Minister Jessica Rosencrantz said.
"The focus should be on the expenditure side, where the volume needs to go down" and the national contribution "needs to go down", she added.
Mr Costa does not only have to contend with the frugals' demands.
France, the second-biggest EU economy and a net contributor to the budget, argues the bloc needs sufficient means to match the rising challenges it faces.
The latest negotiating ⁠proposal for the European Union's next long-term budget is "deeply disappointing", the French presidency said.
"It ‌falls ⁠well short of what is needed, particularly on the Common Agricultural Policy, notably ‌to guarantee income support for farmers," ⁠the presidency ‌said in a statement.
"As it ⁠stands, ‌this proposal from the president of the European ⁠Council does not provide ⁠a basis for an agreement," it added.
Meanwhile, 17 countries from southern, central and eastern Europe have formed a group known as the "Friends of Cohesion" and are pushing for greater funding to support agriculture and regional development.

articles.title_orig: Shaking reported in Australia after magnitude 6.8 earthquake rocks Timor-Leste, Pacific Ring of Fire
articles.title_zh: Shaking reported in Australia after magnitude 6.8 earthquake rocks Timor-Leste, Pacific Ring of Fire
articles.content_orig:
While you may think quakes are a western US problem, some of the largest temblors in US history have happened in the East.
DILI, TIMOR-LESTE — A magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck the Banda Sea about 65 miles northeast of Timor-Leste in Southeast Asia just after 4:30 a.m. ET (6:30 p.m. local time), according to the USGS.
MAGNITUDE 4.2 EARTHQUAKE SHAKES LOS ANGELES FOLLOWING FLURRY OF SEISMIC ACTIVITY ACROSS CENTRAL CALIFORNIA
(FOX Weather / FOX Weather)
The Southeast Asian nation shares the island of Timor with Indonesia, north of Australia .
The quake's epicenter was nearly 90 miles below the surface but was felt in the capital of Dili, as well as Darwin, Australia, some 400 miles to the southeast.
An aerial image shows the view of the city in Dili, East Timor on September 12, 2024.
((Photo by Yasuyoshi CHIBA / AFP) (Photo by YASUYOSHI CHIBA/AFP via Getty Images) / Getty Images)
There were no immediate reports of damage or injuries.
Timor-Leste sits along the Pacific Ring of Fire, a 25,000-mile belt of volcanoes and earthquake zones surrounding much of the Pacific Ocean , where about 90% of the world's earthquakes occur.

articles.title_orig: Russian missiles hit Poland: What happened, and could NATO respond?
articles.title_zh: Russian missiles hit Poland: What happened, and could NATO respond?
articles.content_orig:
Security cameras captured the moment a suspected Russian missile struck Polish territory during an attack on Ukraine on Friday. Poland’s government says it may have been hit by two missiles and a jet-powered drone.
The incident, which took place as European troops held military drills in the country and as the United States pushes to revive talks on ending the war in Ukraine, have raised questions about whether the strike was deliberate.
So what happened, and does this mean Russia has struck Poland, a NATO member?
Poland’s Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference in Warsaw that two missiles and a jet-powered drone fell on Polish territory during Russia’s overnight attack on November 20. The missiles came down at Nowy Lipowiec and Rudnik nad Sanem, while the jet-powered drone fell at Molodycz, all in the country’s southeast.
One missile is believed to have crashed about 35km (22 miles) from where European troops’ military exercises were taking place. A Kh-101 cruise missile went down about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border, and what officials believe was a jet-powered drone hit about 30km (20 miles) from the border. No immediate injuries or damage were reported.
That night, Russia launched one of its heaviest bombardments of Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 400 drones and at least 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, some with cluster warheads. At least eight civilians were killed and more than two dozen were wounded.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared “we are dealing with an intentional provocation” by Russia. He said the incident was likely timed to coincide with the European military exercises in Poland. The unprecedented two-week exercise began on November 9 in southeastern Poland and is preparing forces for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine to help stabilise the country and rebuild its military.
Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at the Clinton Institute, University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera that the incident “fits into a pattern going back for months” of Russia “testing how far they can go”.
“A few months ago, it was flying the drones into airspace , and indeed a couple of times they flew fighter jets across the border into the Baltic states,” he said. “You just test how NATO responds.”
This time, he said, Moscow had “gone a bit further”. “You lob a couple of missiles across and a drone” near where 11 countries are holding exercises.
The Polish Air Force had launched preventive air patrols on September 17 aimed at securing the eastern part of Polish airspace following repeated incursions in the previous weeks.
Harry Nedelcu, partner and senior director for geopolitics at Rasmussen Global, said the testing has not been limited to Poland.
“During the war, there’s been repeated instances of Russia testing NATO allies – Poland, Romania and also non-NATO Moldova as well, which is experiencing – especially over the last few months – increasing numbers of drones and missiles flying over its territory and airspace,” he told Al Jazeera.
He linked the incursions to one of Moscow’s core war aims. “One of the key goals in Ukraine that Russia has had in the full-scale invasion, that has lasted almost five years now, has been to prevent Ukraine from being a part of NATO,” he said. “So their goal clearly is to undermine NATO, to do everything possible to undermine it.
“What Russia is doing with these missiles, drones, that sometimes find their way into NATO territory, tests NATO just under the radar of Article 5 to see how far can they push things. How far can they take hybrid warfare?”
Under Article 5 , each member of the NATO alliance understands that if one of them is the “victim of an armed attack, each and every other member of the alliance will consider this act of violence as an armed attack against all members”.
At a meeting on Thursday with European leaders in Germany’s capital, Berlin, US President Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said he believes Russia would be “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine.
Kushner and fellow special envoy Steve Witkoff have been holding talks with Ukraine and Russia in recent days, in a push for peace which has been viewed as sidelining Ukraine’s European allies.
Following the Berlin meeting, French President Emmanuel Macron said Ukraine’s membership of NATO should be considered again, prompting Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov to push back.
Ryabkov said any form of “quasi membership” for Kyiv of the Western ‌military alliance was totally unacceptable for Moscow, Russian state media reported.
Lucas said the timing of the missile incursion into Polish territory now is very likely tied to the ongoing US-led peace talks.
“The Russians cannot be seen to go through talks and completely exclude Europe,” he said. He described the Kremlin’s push for a “Europe-wide security architecture” as a way to avoid discussing a ceasefire or security guarantees for Ukraine.
“Rather than having a strong Europe at the talks, they want to try to divide Europe, they want to try to unsettle Europe, they want to try to scare Europe,” he said.
He also pointed to Ukraine’s recent strikes on the Kerch Bridge , which links occupied Crimea to Russia. He said these were seen as “a very serious attack on Russian capabilities” with “severe political, military and economic consequences”.
The latest Russian bombardment follows President Vladimir Putin’s pledge to retaliate against those strikes.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the missile incident a “grave violation” of Poland’s airspace. On X, he said the incident was “clearly dangerous” and a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. Rutte is expected to visit Poland this weekend.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it “utterly unacceptable”. Germany’s Foreign Ministry called it “yet another example of Russia’s ongoing provocations”.
US President Donald Trump had played down earlier incursions hours before. “Putin has been landing drones in Poland and a couple of little missiles, by mistake,” he said.
Nedelcu said Warsaw’s reaction was “definitely a strong one”, with Polish officials “drawing a parallel between the fact that actually around the same time there were exercises by the Coalition of the Willing [those countries willing to provide support to Ukraine] nearby, and that this may have not been a coincidence”.
He said Poland is now “asking for more NATO support under this Eastern Sentry mission that already exists”.
“It’s not if, but what form that additional support will take – maybe an airborne early warning aircraft, or something of the sort,” he said.
“But what they have stopped short of is invoking Article 4,” he added, referring to the clause under which allies consult each other before invoking Article 5. “It’s unclear whether this was at their own volition. Maybe perhaps allies don’t want to use it too often, because Article 4 is also quite serious. It has been invoked not often, and it loses its value if it’s constantly invoked.”
Lucas said the public condemnation from European leaders was itself the message to Moscow. “It’s a signal to the Russians: look, we know what you’re doing, we see what you’re doing here,” he said.
“But you’re not going to run it up into an all-out military confrontation over a couple of missiles.”
He said he expects the response to be “defensive”, built on “preparedness” of ground forces, air, naval and cyber-defence, and defence against disinformation. “These will be the most intense preparations you will have had, certainly since the 1980s and possibly well before that,” he said.
On the same day, Denmark took action on a separate front. It announced that it was expelling Russia’s defence attache after Danish intelligence concluded that Moscow had orchestrated a plot to assassinate Ukrainian-American rapper Kyivstoner during a concert near Copenhagen.

articles.title_orig: Walmart shoppers stocked up on emergency supplies after series of tech outages: report
articles.title_zh: Walmart shoppers stocked up on emergency supplies after series of tech outages: report
articles.content_orig:
Walmart said U.S. shoppers stocked up on bottled water, propane and camping gear amid panic buying after a string of recent technology outages.
Walmart shoppers were stocking up on numerous emergency supplies following a series of technology outages that disrupted day-to-day activities and alarmed Americans across the country.
Shoppers loaded their carts with propane, bottled water and camping gear, a Walmart spokesperson told Reuters.
"We have seen a small amount of that. Certainly, categories like jug bottled water or propane are selling at higher comps with that concern, but it’s really relatively small to our overall business. It’s worth noting that oftentimes when we see that, it’s a pull forward of future demand," Walmart's Chief Financial Officer John David Rainey told Yahoo Finance.
The retailer also raised its annual sales and profit forecasts on Thursday, anticipating growth in its delivery and membership as it prepares for the holiday shopping season.
COSTCO SEES PANIC BUYING SURGE AFTER TECH OUTAGES, REPORT SAYS
Walmart shoppers were stocking up on numerous emergency supplies following a series of technology outages. (Christopher Dilts/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Walmart is the largest retailer to report the uptick in emergency supply purchases, but other companies said they experienced similar sales in response to the outages.
Costco and Tractor Supply are among the other retailers to see an increase in demand amid a wave of apparent panic buying.
Mizuho Securities analyst David Bellinger said that the string of technology disruptions led to a sudden surge in emergency preparedness shopping at Costco.
About 21 of the 26 high-ticket generators Costco offers on its website were completely sold out as of Sunday night, according to a note released by Mizuho Securities on Monday.
Among the wiped-out inventory were massive whole-home backup systems priced as high as nearly $7,000.
Walmart shoppers stocked up on propane, bottled water and camping gear. (REUTERS/Mike Blake / Reuters)
"Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights , and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at [Costco]," Mizuho Securities analyst David Bellinger said in the note.
The buying spree has helped put Costco on pace for rare double-digit U.S. sales growth this month, marking a level not seen since mid-2022.
Alongside backup generators, shoppers are also aggressively "pantry-loading" on bulk essentials ahead of the holiday season , the report said.
WALMART RAISES FULL-YEAR OUTLOOK AS WEALTHIER SHOPPERS FUEL SALES GROWTH
Costco and Tractor Supply are among the other retailers to see an increase in demand for emergency supplies. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg / Getty Images)
GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO BY CLICKING HERE
Bellinger raised his price target on Costco shares from $1,100 to $1,150 on the back of the heightened demand.
Meanwhile, Tractor Supply said sales of products like generators, liquid storage tanks and propane accessories are trending higher this year, the company told Bloomberg News. For the first time, shoppers are buying these products at a higher rate than across other product groups.
This comes shortly after a series of disruptions hit the U.S. within days, including a Microsoft outage, a nationwide ground stop caused by an air traffic control failure, a United Airlines technology breakdown and software problems that disrupted some JPMorgan Chase services.
Fox Business' Sophia Compton and Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: There could be serious money in being a manager at your local Target or Sweetgreen
articles.title_zh: There could be serious money in being a manager at your local Target or Sweetgreen
articles.content_orig:
Early in her Target career, Brooke Pratt wondered whether shoppers mistook her for an hourly worker as she helped restock shelves.
She was actually a department manager, earning substantially more than she had in her previous job, an entry-level desk position at a public-relations firm.
"I was thinking, this isn't too bad," Pratt told Business Insider. "I'm putting cereal on the shelf, and I'm making this kind of money. It's pretty cool."
Pratt, 34, is now a store director overseeing 350 team members and 10 department managers at one of Target's largest locations, in Chaska, Minnesota.
Though a Target spokesperson said employees aren't permitted to disclose their salary, the retailer recently advertised a role in Minnesota with the same title, offering $106,000 to $212,000 in annual base pay. The spokesperson said store directors are also eligible to receive an annual bonus and stock equity.
The six-figure salaries that some managers in retail, hospitality, and other service industries now command suggest that leadership sees them as on par with their white-collar managerial counterparts. The higher pay comes at a time, though, when some tech leaders are questioning whether they need so many middle layers in the first place.
Companies including Meta and Block have been cutting their managerial ranks in recent years, arguing that layers of bosses slow decision-making. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong has said org chart layers impose a "coordination tax. "
Meanwhile, Walmart increased pay, annual stock grants, and potential bonuses last year for about 440 of its market managers, who oversee around a dozen stores. Top earners can now make as much as $620,000 in total compensation , up from about $569,000 previously.
Salad chain Sweetgreen has said it plans to introduce a 2027 total compensation plan that could pay some managers of its top-performing locations more than $200,000 a year , part of a broader retention effort.
Similar pay ranges are on offer across other labor-intensive industries. Examples include $200,000 to $300,000 for a general manager at a car dealership in Illinois and about $117,000 to $195,000 for an Apple store leader in California.
The cost of getting management wrong can be especially high in big-box retail, where managers are expected to run increasingly sophisticated operations across physical stores and online orders, said Scott Benedict, a retail consultant who worked in merchandising and e-commerce at Walmart and Sam's Club.
"There's a difference between finding a warm body and finding a leader of the caliber that you need to run what in some cases can be a $100 million or more business," he said, referring to annual sales at a single big-box location.
The pressure can also be intense at a single restaurant.
On a recent Friday morning, two online orders for 50 salads apiece came in back-to-back at a Sweetgreen in Chicago, where Ramsess Salazar, 48, oversees 26 employees who serve several hundred customers a day. With fewer people on the floor than usual, the general manager said he split his team between the digital rush and in-store guests. He then told everyone to stay calm and keep pushing.
"I have stress as well, but I cannot show it to them," Salazar said, adding that about 90 minutes later they were laughing about how many salads they had made.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Another time, a walk-in cooler broke down before lunch at a Sweetgreen in Boston, leaving Salazar with a 100-plus-salad corporate order to fill. He said he rerouted that day's delivery to a nearby sister location's cooler while a technician repaired the broken one.
The value that managers provide in consumer-facing businesses goes beyond solving crises. They often see problems and opportunities as they unfold — from a menu item that isn't selling to a staffing or service issue — and have to respond before headquarters can.
Joe de la Torre, 25, is the general manager of Crush Yard's Nashville location, a 34,000-square-foot entertainment venue offering pickleball, golf simulators, food and drinks, and other games and activities. He oversees six direct reports and 33 hourly employees, helping to run an operation that attracts between 500 and 2,000 visitors a day. De la Torre said he keeps close tabs on the facility, walking around to ensure it meets the company's standards for cleanliness, customer service, and the overall guest experience. He also sometimes helps resolve customer disputes, including disagreements among pickleball players. He then shares his observations with Crush Yard's vice president of operations.
"You get to see all fronts of the business," said de la Torre. He said he makes $84,000 a year in base salary, plus a bonus, which he estimated could bring his annual compensation to as much as $150,000.
Proximity to day-to-day operations can give service-industry managers local knowledge and influence over workers that headquarters can't easily replicate, said Raffaella Sadun, a Harvard Business School professor. In many tech companies, by contrast, leaders believe digital tools and AI can move information without a human in the middle.
That offers a lesson for white-collar managers , Sadun said: Stay close to clients and the work — and raise insights that headquarters can't see on a dashboard.
The work of a frontline manager can be decidedly unglamorous. It often means spending nearly all day on one's feet, pitching in when staffers call out, wearing a uniform, and working nights and weekends.
Pratt, the Target store director, wears tops in the retailer's signature red while on the job, and carries a walkie-talkie throughout her shift to stay in constant contact with her staff. She's also certified to use the store's powered equipment, including a forklift, and fills in for junior colleagues when needed.
"It doesn't matter really what level you are," said Pratt, who added that she learned about leadership while serving as a cheerleading team captain in college. "We all work together as a team to get something done."

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Stock Is Down 35% From Its High. History Suggests a $5,000 Investment Now Will Be Worth This Much by 2028.
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Is Down 35% From Its High. History Suggests a $5,000 Investment Now Will Be Worth This Much by 2028.
articles.content_orig:
By Keithen Drury – Nov 21, 2026 at 4:55AM EST
10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›
Nvidia ( NVDA -14.01% ) stock has gotten slammed over the past few weeks. With former CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang resigning from his position, the market has grown uncertain about Nvidia's future. Furthermore, some of Nvidia's practices have drawn increased scrutiny, which is also adding to fears.
After the sell-off, Nvidia is down over 35% from its all-time high. Since the AI arms race kicked off in 2023, this is now the deepest sell-off Nvidia has seen, just surpassing the tariff-fear sell-off in April 2025. The market has made its opinion known, but does Nvidia actually deserve to be sold off this much? Or is this a generational buying opportunity?
Let's take a look at where the stock could be by 2028, and if now is the perfect time to buy.
With Nvidia's sell-off, it's now down over $2 trillion from its all-time high market cap. So, is Jensen Huang really worth $2 trillion to Nvidia's market cap?
I think the market has way overblown this sell-off. Nvidia’s visionary leader definitely helped shape and drive the company. However, there are still thousands of employees who run the day-to-day operations and designs that Huang had nothing to do with. The real risk is if these employees start to quit or resign from their roles and that knowledge is lost. If there is a mass exodus from Nvidia alongside Huang, that could represent a huge risk for investors.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26
Until we're a few months past Huang's resignation, the market is likely to stay cautious, which is one reason why Nvidia's stock price is down.
Another is the future. Huang's vision for where AI computing and GPUs will go placed Nvidia in a leadership role in the AI build-out. That will have driven product development over the next couple of years, but what comes after that is unknown. This is where a new CEO will need to have a great technical mind and vision for what's coming next. The wrong person at the helm could cause Nvidia's leadership position to collapse in the future if they cannot replicate Huang’s success.
As a result, the market is once again discounting the stock until a new leader is selected.
Lastly, there are concerns that Nvidia’s chips are potentially circumventing export restrictions to China, with some restricted products funneled through Southeast Asian countries, before eventually making their way into China. These are all allegations right now, but Nvidia hasn't been cleared of any wrongdoing yet, so once again, the market is discounting the stock.
Nvidia has a lot of unknowns right now, and the market has kept it in a low-valued spot as a result. The question is, if these are resolved, what could it be worth?
Nvidia has guided for 75% revenue growth in fiscal year (FY) 2028 (ending January 2028), thanks to the strength of the AI build-out. That's up from the 70% guidance given last quarter. With Nvidia estimated to generate around $424 billion in revenue this year, that would indicate revenue of $742 billion next year. At Nvidia's 62% profit margin, the company would generate $460 billion in profits.
Even if the stock traded at the same trailing earnings multiple it does now, that would give it a market cap of $7.4 trillion -- more than doubling today's levels and turning $5,000 into at least $10,000.

As a result, the market could value it like any other big tech stock and price it around 20 to 25 times earnings. That would result in an even larger market cap and make Nvidia a no-brainer buy today.

articles.title_orig: Cop31 live: world urged to avoid one of ‘most disappointing Cops ever’ as talks stretch past deadline
articles.title_zh: Cop31 live: world urged to avoid one of ‘most disappointing Cops ever’ as talks stretch past deadline
articles.content_orig:
Panama's Environment Minister is pushing for language on fossil fuels to be in the final agreement
Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock, having run more than 24 hours into overtime as countries remain unable to agree on a new global climate deal.
In a late intervention on Friday, a group of countries led by France and Panama pushed back against the draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.
This still remains the main sticking point, along with a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptation - but the EU has previously said it would not support this.
Negotiating teams due to fly out on Sunday morning are now moving their flights to Monday in a sign that a deal is not in sight.
Not all countries have the funding or capacity to do this, and at some point the meeting could lose the critical number of nations needed to pass any global agreement.
This means the summit would end with no deal and have to be suspended. This has only happened once before in the 24 years countries have been meeting.
More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.
She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.
For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - acknowledges that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".
Beyond this point scientists warn , external that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
The BBC understands that a number of other EU nations were asked to join the rebellion but declined, considering it unhelpful to negotiations.
Although one lead negotiator said he sympathised: "How can you have a climate agreement with no mention of the cause."
But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back.
He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.
Away from COP, renewable energy is growing at unprecedented rates. For the first time this year a modern renewable source - solar panels - contributed the largest share of global energy demand growth, outstripping oil and gas , external .
The International Energy Agency also warned this week that the longer disruption to fuel supplies through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran War, the stronger the incentive to switch to electricity powered by renewables.
Although, this week US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed at a meeting in Shenzhen to increase oil production in the face of fuel supply disruption.
It is understood that one proposal is to keep fossil fuels off the table in exchange for Saudi Arabia and other petro-states signing up to a pledge for 35% of their energy consumption to come from electricity by 2035.
This does not solve one of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money.
Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (Â£91bn) by 2035 - that has now been removed.
"We did not come here to beg we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.
Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.
"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.
These groups are normally highly critical of the process for not moving fast enough. But it seems that Turkey have been particularly unpopular as hosts after their lead negotiator walked out of some crucial negotiations leaving many countries feeling "disrespected" said one observer.

articles.title_orig: Using AI, mathematician claims to have solved one of math’s great mysteries
articles.title_zh: Using AI, mathematician claims to have solved one of math’s great mysteries
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic just went public with a major IPO this week
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.
Levent AlpÃ¶ge said , external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut , that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. AlpÃ¶ge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
AlpÃ¶ge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," AlpÃ¶ge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete textual proof that AlpÃ¶ge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday , external that verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.
OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.
The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths , external and physics , external .
A group of maths scholars said , external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released , external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine war briefing: European leaders react with anger and alarm after Russian missiles crash in Poland
articles.title_zh: Ukraine war briefing: European leaders react with anger and alarm after Russian missiles crash in Poland
articles.content_orig:
Russian missile and drone incident during western military exercises a ‘grave violation’ of Polish airspace, says Nato’s Rutte. What we know on day 1,732
Russian missiles and a drone crashing in Poland during major military exercises being held in the Nato country have been described by European leaders as a “provocation” and an “irresponsible gamble” that will only further isolate Moscow and strengthen the west’s resolve to support Ukraine. Nato secretary general Mark Rutte called the development a “grave violation” of Polish airspace. “This incident is clearly dangerous – a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine,” Rutte, who is expected to go to Poland this weekend in response, wrote on X.
On Friday, two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in the Nato country, according to Polish officials. The missiles hit during Russian air attacks on Ukraine . Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, said he believed it was “not accidental” that the incident took place on the same day as the joint military exercises involving troops from 11 countries in the “coalition of the willing”. The incidents were reported in Nowy Lipowiec, Mołodycz and Rudnik nad Sanem in south-eastern Poland, between 30 miles (50km) and 60 miles from Nowa Dęba, where the military exercises are taking place.
Calling the incident “an intentional provocation” by Russia, Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, said he had spoken with Rutte who agreed with him that “it does not seem to be a coincidence” that the attack took place on the night before the drills. “It clearly shows … that coming months … will certainly pose great challenges for all of us,” he said. The incident came as the defence ministers of Britain, France, Estonia, Lithuania and Poland visited Nowa Deba to tour the training site. About 2,800 soldiers from 10 countries are training at the camp, backed by several thousand Polish troops handling logistics.
After Moscow pounded Ukraine with massive strikes Friday, French president Emmanuel Macron said Russia’s actions in Ukraine and Europe were an “irresponsible gamble” that would increase the resolve of Europeans. “By escalating its war of aggression against Ukraine and also pursuing an aggressive agenda on European soil, Russia is making an irresponsible gamble that can only further isolate it and strengthen the resolve and unity of Europeans,” he said on X.
Donald Trump has told reporters that Putin wants to end Russia’s war against Ukraine . In his first public remarks since his trilateral meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump appeared to sidestep a question about whether he sees Putin as a friend of the US. “I can’t speak to America,” he said, without expounding, before shifting to his “very good” personal relationship with Putin. “He’d love to end the war,” Trump said of his Russian counterpart. But “you have two guys that don’t know how to end it. We’re trying to help them.”
Reacting to Trump’s comments, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, called Putin a “killer” in an interview broadcast by CNN on Friday. “For us he’s an enemy, and of course, for us, he is a killer. And I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer,” Zelensky told CNN.
Earlier, Zelenskyy said Russia’s latest attack on Ukraine was “one of the largest” since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022 , with at least eight people killed and nearly 30 injured in Ukraine on Friday. “The Russians spread this attack across many cities and regions of Ukraine. Absolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure – things that literally sustain people’s lives,” he said. Zelenskyy said Putin went ahead with the strike after “weak meetings” with the US president, Donald Trump, and China’s Xi Jinping, and his “failure to attempt to somehow redraw the world”.
Denmark’s foreign minister on Friday said Russia’s defence attache in Copenhagen will be expelled after Moscow was suspected of being behind an attempted killing of a US-Ukrainian rapper . “We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark,” Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference. The expulsion will happen within seven days. Rasmussen also said that Denmark was considering suspending Schengen visas to Russians. Danish police said they had averted an attempt by Russian intelligence services ⁠to kill the US-Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner in September before a planned performance in Denmark.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street suffers historic losses as Dow, S&P 500 plunge into correction territory
articles.title_zh: Wall Street suffers historic losses as Dow, S&P 500 plunge into correction territory
articles.content_orig:
FOX Business anchor Gerri Willis has the latest on the massive sell-off in the U.S. stock market amid a widespread artificial intelligence stock sell-off on 'Special Report.'
U.S. stocks plunged Friday in one of Wall Street's worst trading sessions in years, when a massive sell-off in artificial intelligence companies wiped out the Nasdaq's gains for the year and pushed the Dow and S&P 500 into correction territory.
The historic sell-off sent major U.S. indexes sharply lower, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average falling nearly 950 points, while the S&P 500 dropped 3.7% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite plunged 5.28%.
Both the Dow and S&P 500 entered correction territory, meaning they had fallen at least 10% from their recent record highs.
The steep decline erased the Nasdaq's gains for the year, marking its second-largest single-day point drop on record.
ANTHROPIC'S $1.5 TRILLION IPO SETS OFF A FRESH WAVE OF TECH WEALTH HEADING FOR SOUTH FLORIDA
U.S. stocks plunged Friday in one of Wall Street's worst trading sessions in years as a massive sell-off in artificial intelligence companies sent major indexes sharply lower. (Reuters/Brendan McDermid / Reuters)
"It was a brutal day in the stock market with AI fears taking center stage," FOX Business anchor Gerri Willis reported Friday on "Special Report."
Investors directed much of their selling toward technology companies, putting additional pressure on the Nasdaq, Willis noted.
"Investors saved their real wrath for the tech-heavy Nasdaq," Willis said.
The massive sell-off came amid mounting concerns about the AI boom, with some of the industry's biggest names suffering steep losses, including chip-making giant Nvidia and newly public AI developer Anthropic.
HOLIDAY AIRFARES HIT HIGHEST LEVELS IN A DECADE AS JET FUEL PRICES SURGE
Wall Street suffered steep losses Friday as concerns over artificial intelligence stocks wiped out the Nasdaq's gains for the year and pushed the Dow and S&P 500 into correction territory. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Nvidia shares tumbled approximately 14%, while Anthropic fell about 9% during its second trading session as a public company.
Friday's declines came despite strong earnings from Nvidia and a highly anticipated stock market debut for Anthropic, which failed to ease investor concerns about soaring AI valuations and spending.
Recent technology disruptions affecting major companies and institutions over the past 10 days may have contributed to investor unease, Willis said.
"Much of the investor anxiety [has been] spiking this week on reports of tech meltdowns at companies as diverse as United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase," Willis said.
ANTHROPIC IPO TURNS THOUSANDS OF TECH WORKERS INTO OVERNIGHT MILLIONAIRES, REPORTS SAY
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei speaks Thursday during its initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City. (Brendan McDermid/Reuters / Reuters)
The historic losses capped a particularly difficult week for Wall Street , with the S&P 500 posting its worst weekly percentage decline since April 2025, while the Nasdaq recorded its largest weekly percentage loss since March 2020.
The Dow also suffered its steepest weekly decline since April 2025, according to Reuters.
Friday marked the S&P 500's seventh consecutive losing session, its longest losing streak since February 2020.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell nearly 950 points Friday as Wall Street suffered a broad sell-off driven by weakness in technology stocks. (Yuki Iwamura/AFP via Getty Images / Getty Images)
The market turmoil also sent Wall Street's closely watched volatility index, commonly known as the VIX or "fear gauge," to its highest closing level since April 2025.

LIMA, Peru – A magnitude 6.7 earthquake struck Peru just after 7:09 p.m. local time on Friday, shaking the region northeast of the capital city of Lima, which is home to roughly 10 million people.
According to the U.S. Geological Survey, the quake hit at a depth of about 67 miles and was centered roughly 5.6 miles northeast of Carhuamayo.

articles.title_orig: Japan wary of U.S., Russia and China holding regular summits
articles.title_zh: Japan wary of U.S., Russia and China holding regular summits
articles.content_orig:
After the United States, China and Russia held an unprecedented trilateral summit on Thursday, Japan is concerned that the trilateral framework may become a regular occurrence.
On the heels of the summit between U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi held telephone talks with Trump to affirm close cooperation between Japan and the United States.
At a news conference in Tokyo on Friday, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara stressed, “We’ll communicate closely with our allies and like-minded nations and work to maintain and strengthen a free and open international order.”
Japan is eager to maintain the existing international order, including by strengthening the rule of law.
In a joint peace declaration released after the summit, the U.S., Chinese and Russian leaders confirmed their commitment to “maintaining strategic stability and international security.” A Japanese government official said, “We were relieved that nothing major was decided at the summit.”
Still, there are concerns in Japan that the three major powers may hold summits on a regular basis. A senior Foreign Ministry official said, “That all depends on how serious Trump is (about the three-way framework).”
At a U.S.-China summit in September, Trump noted that the two countries were allies during World War II. At Thursday’s meeting, Xi said that the three nations fought side by side in the war against fascism, and Putin said that their shared victory in the war united them.
“We cannot overlook the fact that China and Russia are bringing up such ties,” said a high-ranking Japanese government official.
The peace declaration also warned that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies “must not abuse their jurisdiction.” The ICC, based in The Hague in the Netherlands, has issued an arrest warrant for Putin over his country’s invasion of Ukraine, and has launched an investigation into alleged war crimes by U.S. military personnel.
As Japan supports the ICC, headed by Tomoko Akane, a Japanese national, the disagreement between Tokyo and Washington over the court may become a source of friction.
Speaking to reporters after the phone talks with Trump on Thursday evening, Takaichi admitted that Japan and the United States have different views. However, she stressed, “Japan’s position is to strengthen the rule of law while cooperating with relevant countries.”
In her message to an international conference on Ukraine held the same day, Takaichi said that any attempts to unilaterally change the status quo by force must not be tolerated.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Trump says next move on Iran may not come until 2027 as Tehran denies chemical weapons claim
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Trump says next move on Iran may not come until 2027 as Tehran denies chemical weapons claim
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump boards Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Md., on Nov. 16, 2026.
President Donald Trump suggested he is putting off any major decisions on Iran until 2027, amid reports that he’s considering renewed major operations in the war that continues despite repeated promises that it’ll end soon.
Speaking to Reuters on whether new major strikes are possible—the U.S. has engaged in limited strikes on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz—Trump, who was en route to Washington following his trip to China, said, “Well, I’ll talk to you about it after the beginning of the year.” He added: “We’ve got time.”
Trump made similar comments in other interviews. “We’ll see what happens after January 1st," the U.S. President told Fox News in an interview that aired on Thursday, just before his summit with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin . He also told Axios in a phone call Thursday that he was “not rushing into any decision” on Iran.
The President initially promised that the war with Iran would only take weeks, but it has dragged on to nearly nine months, though major hostilities have subsided. Trump has previously said that the war would end immediately after the Nov. 3 midterm elections , but the impasse between Iran and the U.S. remained. And in the past weeks, he’s alternated between publicly threatening Tehran and holding off on authorizing new strikes at the request of American allies in the Gulf .
Israel has reportedly tried to convince Trump of a new joint strike. The New York Times reported that the U.S. President is considering a new round of extensive military strikes on Iran, after Tel Aviv warned of Tehran’s “success in rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals and advancing its chemical and biological weapons programs.” Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli Prime Minister whose premiership is in limbo , is reportedly pushing for a four- to seven-day airstrike campaign on Iran.
Axios reported, citing unnamed sources , that the White House sought input from the Pentagon and intelligence experts on how Iran would respond to the strike scenarios prepared by the U.S. military. Axios also reported that any U.S. campaign would involve Israel and could include strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities such as Pickaxe Mountain, energy and other infrastructure, and Iranian military and civilian leaders.
The U.S. midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of Congress as the American public largely rebuked Trump and the Republican Party following their handling of the Iran war and the economic fallout it caused, could complicate decisionmaking. Before the Nov. 3 elections, Trump said that Iran was willing to strike a deal, but after the GOP’s stunning losses, which Iranian leaders celebrated , the Administration’s messaging pivoted to maintaining economic sanctions and the blockade on Iran.
Vice President J.D. Vance has blamed the war for the GOP’s election losses, but still appeared to defend the President’s foreign policy on Iran . The Vice President earlier said there was no difference between the President and members of his Administration on the war, but as Vance voiced his misgivings, Trump ordered the Vice President to shift his focus away from Iran diplomatic negotiations and toward domestic policies.
Trump has a small window to push through further military action against Iran before the newly elected Democrats take office in January. On Thursday, the GOP-led U.S. Senate rejected a measure aimed at curbing the war .
In the interview with Fox News, Trump said he thinks people should not be alarmed by reports of a planned “ dirty bomb ” attack on Washington, D.C. A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives like dynamite with radioactive material.
“If it does happen, we wipe them out,” Trump said.
Trump acknowledged , however, that intelligence indicated Tehran is potentially interested in biological weapons. “Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear,” he said, referring to the damage that the U.S. has claimed it dealt to Iran’s nuclear facilities .
Iran’s foreign ministry refuted Trump’s recent statements. “The allegations keep changing, but the underlying narrative remains disturbingly familiar,” spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X .  “Once again, the world is apparently expected to suffer a bout of collective amnesia."
Baqaei then referred to how the U.S. justified its invasion of Iraq in 2003, alleging that the government of the late Saddam Hussein was developing weapons of mass destruction, which subsequent investigations found to be untrue.
“We find ourselves facing ominous new allegations,” Baqaei said, “and a narrative that appears to be following the same fraudulent script.”

articles.content_orig:
Adam Feuerstein, a senior writer and biotech columnist, is the author of Adam’s Biotech Scorecard , a subscriber-only newsletter about the crossroads of drug development, business, Wall Street, and biotechnology.
Adam Feuerstein is a senior writer and biotech columnist, reporting on the crossroads of drug development, business, Wall Street, and biotechnology. He is also a co-host of the weekly biotech podcast The Readout Loud and author of the newsletter Adam’s Biotech Scorecard. You can reach Adam on Signal at stataf.54.
The Food and Drug Administration said Friday that it had rejected a cell therapy intended for patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy developed by Capricor Therapeutics.
The decision to block the treatment, called deramiocel, from reaching the market should have been an easy one for regulators to make. The targeted patient population — teenagers and young men with Duchenne who had already lost the ability to walk — have few treatment options today. Deramiocel didn’t help them either. Capricor conducted two randomized clinical trials . Both failed to show deramiocel could stave off heart failure or preserve muscle function in their arms.
But nothing is straightforward when it comes to regulating drugs for Duchenne, a progressive, muscle-wasting disease.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market News, Nov. 20, 2026: Tech Rout Deepens as Nvidia, Anthropic Slide
articles.title_zh: Stock Market News, Nov. 20, 2026: Tech Rout Deepens as Nvidia, Anthropic Slide
articles.content_orig:
Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.
The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.
Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.
The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.
The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.
Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO)  price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.
Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.
Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.
But tech stocks more broadly also fell.
Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.
Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.
South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic may have solved major maths problem Reimann hypothesis
articles.title_zh: Anthropic may have solved major maths problem Reimann hypothesis
articles.content_orig:
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.
Levent Alpöge said on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut , that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete textual proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday that verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.
OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.
The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths and physics .
A group of maths scholars said AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.
