articles.title_orig: Trump considering new Iran strikes as US military warns of strain on forces
articles.title_zh: Trump considering new Iran strikes as US military warns of strain on forces
articles.content_orig:
Saudi-led coalition said it downed three Houthi missiles headed for Riyadh after two explosions were heard in the area early on Saturday morning local time, an AFP journalist in the Saudi capital reported.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed (3) ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition said on X.
The blasts came after authorities issued an alert saying the city was "under a hostile aerial threat."
The Saudi civil defense later lifted the alert and declared that "the danger has passed."
Yemen's Houthis said on X that they were striking targets across Saudi Arabia, including in Riyadh.
The incident came after the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis attacked the Red Sea port city of Hodeida and other targets in a "special operation" on Friday.
The Houthis had threatened reprisals.
Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited in neighboring Yemen's civil war, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognized government against the Houthis.
Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming the next Israeli government, vowed Friday not to let coalition-building talks drag on as his wide-ranging bloc faces divisions on the way forward.
The former military chief's remarks appear as a warning to his own camp, which is split over whether to forge alliances with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties, Arab-majority lists, or to form a national unity government that would leave current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the role as a caretaker.
Sources told CBS News this week that Netanyahu is keen to launch a new offensive against Iran in collaboration with the U.S.
"I have no intention of letting this drag on. When the time is right, I will bring a new government before the Knesset for its approval, a good government that I will lead," Eisenkot said in a social media post.
Eisenkot has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu, after the October election failed to deliver a clear majority for either of them. While denying any attempt to force through a coalition, Eisenkot stressed the need to act fast.
"We are in very dangerous territory. The outgoing prime minister is acting in ways we have never seen before," he said. "Military priorities have become entangled with political interests, and the timetable for military operations with the political calendar."
The AFP contributed reporting.
A tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was struck by a projectile Friday, causing a fire onboard the vessel but no injuries, according to a British naval monitor.
The tanker was traveling out of the key waterway when it was struck by an unknown projectile, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center.
The UKMTO earlier reported that a bulk carrier traveling east in the Gulf of Aden, off the southern coast of Yemen, had reported shots being fired in its vicinity by assailants on a small boat.
During Friday's news conference, President Trump said that during his trilateral with Russia's President Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping, the three leaders discussed nuclear responsibilities.
Mr. Trump said they "spoke about the need to cooperate to stop the proliferation of that nuclear threat throughout our planet" and that "in particular, we talked extensively about ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon."
As he lauded slightly lower gas prices during a news conference at the White House on Friday, President Trump said the U.S. wants a "real deal" with Iran, not a "fake" deal.
"They want to make a deal but they don't want to make a deal that's acceptable to me," he said.
"They've been bulls******g people for 51 years," the president said of Iran.
U.S. Central Command denied carrying out any new strikes on Iran's strategic Qeshm Island on Friday after Iran's Tasnim news agency, which is closely linked with the country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said a missile had hit the island in the Strait of Hormuz.
Tasnim said it had no information of any possible damage, and other Iranian media outlets offered more vague details. The semi-official Fars news agency said an explosion was heard in the skies over the island, but that the cause was unknown.
The U.S. has attacked the island several times, most recently on Tuesday with what a military official described to CBS News as precision strikes on an IRGC missile site.
The official said that strike was launched "in self-defense … in response to IRGC aggression targeting U.S. personnel and assets."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said Friday that it had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis.
Saudi Arabia backs Yemen's government in the impoverished nation's more than decade-long civil war against the Iran-backed rebel group.
The latest missiles launched by the Houthis targeted the Jazan region, on the southwest Saudi coast near the border with Yemen, but "air defense intercepted and destroyed" them, according to coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki.
The Houthis struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district earlier this week.
A bulk carrier traveling east in the Gulf of Aden, off the southern coast of Yemen, has reported shots being fired in its vicinity by armed men on a small boat, according to a British naval monitor.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center, which is run by the British navy, said Friday that the ship was traveling eastbound when it was approached "by a dark blue skiff with six unidentified, armed persons on board."
"Four shots were fired in quick succession from the skiff and warning shots were returned by the armed security team onboard the bulk carrier," UKTMO said, adding that there was no damage reported to the vessel or its crew.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis urged people to avoid Riyadh's financial district Friday as the group issued a series of threats against Saudi Arabia.
"We announce that (King Abdullah Financial District) in the Saudi enemy's capital, Riyadh, is a military target for our forces. We therefore call on all employees, workers and citizens to stay away from it immediately," military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X.
In a Telegram post Friday, Saree wrote: "We renew our warning to all investment companies, investors and capital to leave Saudi Arabia immediately and move to safe countries. Saudi Arabia is not safe except for the holy areas in Mecca and Medina."
Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of damaging a skyscraper in Riyadh's financial district with a strike earlier this week.
Israel and the U.S. are considering launching a new assault on Iran in the short term, according to sources familiar with the matter.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's administration is concerned about how rapidly the Iranians are rebuilding their ballistic missile manufacturing capabilities and the pace at which Iran is working to shield its military and nuclear infrastructure from attack by moving it underground, the sources told CBS News.
Months of indirect negotiations between the U.S. and Iran have failed to bring a ceasefire deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran has refused to even discuss its nuclear program unless the U.S. lifts its naval blockade and accepts six other key conditions .
Israel's military is prepared for a new round of fighting with Iran and is in peak defensive posture to respond to any first attack by Iran, the sources told CBS News.
The Netanyahu administration would prefer to launch a new joint operation with the U.S., but the sources told CBS News it remains unclear whether Mr. Trump wants to order new military action, and if so, what kind.
For both Mr. Trump and Netanyahu, who jointly launched the war with Iran almost nine months ago with a massive round of strikes on the Islamic Republic, the window for any new collaborative action may be closing.
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting in the escalating conflict with Iran's Houthi allies warned civilians Friday to leave the area around the key port

articles.title_zh: The Nasdaq Just Had Its 6th Correction in 4 Years. History Says This Is the Likelihood of a Full-Blown Bear Market
articles.content_orig:
By Bram Berkowitz – Nov 20, 2026 at 2:57PM EST
10 stocks we like better than NASDAQ Composite Index ›
Tech stocks are having a brutal November. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -5.28% ) is now down nearly 17% from its Oct. 6 peak. A correction means an index closes at least 10% below its record, while a bear market means a decline of 20% or more.
Several factors are weighing on the tech-heavy Nasdaq, including disappointing earnings from hyperscalers and a Blue Tsunami in the midterm elections that raised concerns about further regulations and restrictions on data centers .
Add in the Jensen Huang scandal and a Federal Reserve leaning toward more interest rate hikes, and investors have plenty to worry about. This is the Nasdaq's sixth correction in four years, which have overall been quite prosperous for investors.
History suggests these are the odds that the correction will turn into a full-blown bear market.
Image source: Getty Images.
As I mentioned, while the stock market has had a terrific four years, it has been volatile and also had its fair share of ups and downs, including five corrections prior to the current one.
As you can see, corrections are more common than one might suspect. In fact, a 2024 Reuters study of LSEG data found that the Nasdaq has experienced 24 corrections over the past 44 years. According to Dow Jones Market Data, the Nasdaq has extended a correction into a bear market about 37% of the time since 1971.
The good news is that the majority of corrections tend to revert back higher. The bad news is that there is still a decent chance that a correction could morph into a full-blown bear market , and the Nasdaq is not far from one as of this writing.
This is the reality for Nasdaq investors. Investing more heavily in tech can yield fantastic gains, but typically entails greater turbulence. History also tells us the Nasdaq has generated fantastic gains. Since the turn of the century, the Nasdaq has generated a total return of 467%, besting the broader benchmark S&P 500's total return of nearly 379%.
This includes the Dot-Com Bubble, in which the Nasdaq lost roughly 77% of its value between 2000 and 2002. So, long-term investors can stay invested in the Nasdaq, but it really depends on your risk tolerance. If you can't handle big swings multiple times a year, then the Nasdaq might not be the right index for you.

articles.title_orig: Trump on gas prices, China summit, war in Iran, and more | Full remarks
articles.title_zh: Trump on gas prices, China summit, war in Iran, and more | Full remarks
articles.content_orig:
Trump, Xi and Putin don't have much to say after their historic meeting.
President Donald Trump is headed back to Washington after a historic trilateral meeting with presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia -- the first-ever sitdown between the three global superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.
Following their meeting, the three leaders released what was described as a symbolic four-point "peace declaration," focusing on reform at the United Nations, oil supply, nuclear risk reduction and opposition to what it called the International Criminal Court's "jurisdiction abuse."
The symbolic peace declaration made no mention of Russia's war with Ukraine, which is in its fifth year, or the war with Iran. Both Russia and China have faced accusations by U.S. and European officials of providing satellite imagery and broader intelligence support to Iran, accusations both countries have denied.
Trump left Shenzhen without taking questions from reporters after the meeting but announced in a post on his social media platform while traveling back to Washington that he would hold a news conference at the White House on Friday.
Here are takeaways from Trump's trip:
The three leaders affirmed their commitment that nuclear war should never be fought but announced no commitments to reduce their respective nuclear arsenals.
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in brief remarks ahead of the meeting. "The power is unbelievable, unthinkable."
"It's not an ​easy thing to do -- give them up," Trump said.
Trump also used the issue of nuclear proliferation to defend the U.S. war with Iran, repeating his assertion that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.
"It's also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That's what we're doing in Iran. We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.
In a joint statement released following the meeting, the three leaders said they had an "in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation" and "committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security."
Trump, Xi, and Putin said the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The "peace declaration" released after the meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran.
"We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That's what pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening," Trump said.
For his part, Putin briefly commented on his escalating war in Ukraine during opening remarks.
"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine. We discussed this yesterday with the Chairman of the People's Republic of China and today at the initiative of the U.S. president, we devoted significant attention to this during our bilateral meeting," the Russian president said, speaking through a translator.
The leaders also declared they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products "for the benefit of all nations" while also reaffirming the importance of the stable flow of energy.
The oil market has been roiled in the nine months of the U.S.'s war with Iran, with the critical waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil supplies has transited under constant threat. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further exacerbated global energy flows.
There were no signs upon conclusion of their meeting that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.
Trump also highlighted that the three would discuss the International Criminal Court, the international body that works to uphold international law and prosecute war crimes. The Trump administration has targeted the ICC and its judges with sanctions and has sharply criticized the body.
"In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nation's sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction," Trump said in his opening remarks.
As part of the peace declaration, the three heads of state "recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction."
ABC News has reached out to the ICC for comment.

articles.title_zh: 10 years on, Britain reopens the Brexit fight — this time embracing the E.U.
articles.content_orig:
President of European Council says EU ‘remains open to have the closest possible relationship’ with the UK
The British prime minister Andy Burnham said his deal with the European Union will add up to £17bn a year to the British economy as he paved the way for even closer ties to Brussels. Burnham said it was a “good day for Britain and a good day for Europe”, as he met EU chiefs in Brussels to announce a package covering food and agriculture exports, emissions trading, and a youth experience scheme which could open the doors for 100,000 young Europeans to temporarily work in the UK, with Britons able to do the same on the continent.
Burnham ‌said Friday’s deal was “probably the limit” of what could be done before the next national election due by mid-2029 , but he envisaged an informal conversation in about a year ‌with the EU about what could be achieved next.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she welcomed Burnham’s willingness to have a broad debate about future relations with the EU. “We are open for brainstorming, and we welcome this brainstorming, so count on us,” she said.
At the summit, postponed from July after the resignation of Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer, ‌the two sides addressed some of the Brexit losses with a package of agreements. The most significant allows cross-border trade in animals, plants and related products, such as sausages or seeds, without the certificates and controls currently required. Britain has estimated this could add up to £5.1bn per year to its economy.
A further agreement will link the emissions trading systems of Britain and the EU, which would exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies. Each side is also set to allow 100,000 young people a year in to work or study for three years.
However, one potential dampener emerged as the 27-nation bloc and London jostled over linking ultimate implementation of the new deals to Britain agreeing to cut university fees for EU students. Britain ⁠prefers to offer only “significantly reduced” fees, and the aim is to resolve the issue within six months.
Retailers and manufacturers have welcomed Andy Burnham’s new trade deal with the European Union as a “big win” but warned they need “clear and early” guidance from government to aid the transition, Press Association reported. The chief executive of the British Retail Consortium (BRC) called the SPS deal a “big win” for UK retailers but warned that businesses need “at least 18 months” to transition to the new arrangements.
Nigel Farage, the veteran anti-EU campaigner and leader of the Reform UK party, said the deal “was about the first steps, incrementally, to taking us back into membership of the European Union,” and again predicted an early election next year. Farage told reporters he would campaign to preserve Brexit. “I am ready for this fight,” he said.
Meanwhile, Denmark’s foreign minister on Friday said Moscow’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Russia was suspected of being behind an attempted assassination of a Ukrainian rapper. “We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark” within seven days, Lars Lokke Rasmussen told a news conference.
Students and young workers have taken to the streets in more than 20 European countries in coordinated protests over the surging cost of living and housing, deteriorating learning conditions and rising military spending. “We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you”, he said.
He also added Denmark was mulling suspending Schengen visas to Russians.
The UK prime minister called the newly agreed post-Brexit reset deal a “win-win” for the UK and the EU, although the level of tuition fees EU students will pay to study at UK universities remains unresolved.
The prime minister met Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president, at the EU-UK summit in Brussels.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage claimed that Andy Burnham’s reset agreements with the EU “was in direct contradiction of the Labour manifesto upon which they were elected in 2024”.
He also said Burnham’s actions “went completely against the pledge that he made to the voters of Makerfield just a few months ago”.
The Reform leader later added: “Burnham’s whole rationale is 73% of the people want to be closer to Europe .
“Well, if you ask me do I want better relations with our European neighbours? Do I think we could have a better trade deal than we’ve got at the moment? I am part of that 73%.
“But what he completely misunderstands is that is not an open ticket to rejoin a significant chunk of the single market today.”
Students and young workers have taken to the streets in more than 20 European countries in coordinated protests over the surging cost of living and housing, deteriorating learning conditions and rising military spending.
Activists from more than 50 groups in countries including Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Portugal , Spain and the UK held rallies on Friday, lighting flares, burning cardboard models of tanks and waving placards, many reading “fight for our future”.
Calling it Europe’s biggest coordinated youth protest of recent years, the Youth Strike coalition said demonstrations were planned in about 400 cities under the slogan “fight for our future, not their wars”.
It made five broad demands, including an end to militarisation and conscription; structural investment in education and welfare; solidarity with Palestine; climate and social justice, and a “radical transformation of the system we live in”.
An Italian organiser, Alessandro di Miceli, said the Europe-wide protests were “to claim our right to a better and dignified future”. Specific demands differed from country to country, he said, but were all “deeply connected between each other”.
A Portuguese organiser, Leonor Chicó, said: “As young people, we know that we must organise and fight for our future, because no one else will do it for us.” Governments “show us every day that the needs of our generation are not their priority”, she said.
Shabbir Lakha from the UK-based Stop The War coalition said the mobilisation was “a crucial step towards building a lasting international movement capable of bringing together young people, students and workers around common demands”.
After weeks of demonstrations across several countries sparked by long-running French school protests , governments are struggling to respond to growing calls for affordable housing, functioning public services and greater social equality.
Speaking to British reporters following the leaders’ lunch, Burnham stressed that nothing would happen in the current parliament that went much beyond this deal.
He said: “There is a clear democratic mandate for what has been done today. It’s in the Labour manifesto… There will be nothing beyond the significance of this in this parliament.”

articles.title_orig: Trump defends Putin ties and accuses Iran of bad faith
articles.title_zh: Trump defends Putin ties and accuses Iran of bad faith
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump has praised his recent trip to China and defended the relationship with his “friend” Vladimir Putin, but questioned whether the Russian president was a friend to the US.
On Friday, during a White House news briefing, Trump was asked about the “friend” remark — made during his historic summit with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping earlier this week — and whether the Russian leader was a friend to the US.
“I can’t speak to America,” Trump told reporters before saying Putin had been “very nice” during what he described as the “Russia hoax” investigation after his 2016 presidential campaign.
“I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship. And it’s actually very good,” Trump added as he talked about Russia’s nuclear weapons capabilities.
“I think it gives us a lot of additional strength,” he said.
Trump also spoke about the historic nature of his meeting with Xi and Putin, praising the “first of its kind trilateral peace agreement”. He said there was “great electricity” between the leaders of the world’s main nuclear powers.
“We had one of the most momentous international summits in many years. That was the first ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China,” Trump said.
“I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that,” he also said.
No major deals were announced from the summit. But Trump, on Friday, played up his agreement with the two leaders to hold future discussions on nuclear proliferation.
The US president’s remarks came during a wide-ranging news conference, where topics from Iran to artificial intelligence were also discussed.
Trump accused Iran of negotiating in bad faith to end the war , which is about to mark its 10-month anniversary.
“They want to make a deal, but they don’t want to make a deal that’s acceptable to me,” he said. “We wanna make a real deal, not a fake deal.”
Trump added: “They’ve been b*********** people for 51 years.”
During the news conference, US Vice President JD Vance and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, both possible 2028 presidential contenders, flanked Trump in the White House press briefing room.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Defence Secretary Hegseth, as well as newly minted White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, were also present.
Trump denied he was upset at Vance for blaming US Republicans’ historic midterm losses on the Iran war, saying, “People that work for me, they have a right to their opinion.”
“I thought his statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing that, if we were asked, I would have said that, would you do it again, and absolutely the answer is yes,” Trump said. “I saw that, but no problem there at all.”
Vance was asked by reporters about his thoughts on his party’s midterm drubbing.
“I think the president is the one who makes the decision. And the president has said he would do it again,” Vance said. “My goal, in my job, is to support the President of the United States.”
Trump also warned US tech companies against building new artificial intelligence data centres overseas. Otherwise, he said, they will face a “tremendous tax”.
“We’re not allowing data centres to go into other countries because China will take all of them”, Trump said. “And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”
Trump did not provide details on how he would enforce such a policy and said he had not yet told his own officials about his plan.
Al Jazeera has reached out to the White House for comment but has not yet heard back.

articles.title_orig: FDA urgently recalls sandwiches over dangerous ‘organism’ linked to fatal infections
articles.title_zh: FDA urgently recalls sandwiches over dangerous ‘organism’ linked to fatal infections
articles.content_orig:
The US Food and Drug Administration has recalled a line of grab-and-go breakfast sandwiches over fears they’re contaminated with a terrifying organism linked to fatal infections, stillbirths, and miscarriages.
Grand Strand Sandwich Company Inc. asked to rip the items from shelves on Thursday after discovering the dangerous contaminant.
Its Lunch Box-branded sandwiches, which were sold in North Carolina, South Carolina, and Virginia, potentially contain Listeria monocytogenes, an organism which can cause the serious infection listeriosis, the FDA announced.
The affected products were distributed between March 2 and Nov. 10 and include:
The sandwiches were sold at convenience stores, vending machines and prison canteens. No illnesses have been linked to the items.
Those with weaker immune systems who contract the bug like young children, elderly people, and pregnant women could face short-term symptoms like high fever, severe headaches, nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain and diarrhea.
Pregnant women could also suffer miscarriages, stillbirths, premature delivery or life-threatening infection of the newborn if the nasty organism infects the fetus.
Anyone who has purchased a recalled item is urged to throw the item away immediately, especially if it could be hiding in the back of a freezer or pantry.
Affected products can be redeemed for a refund if the packaging is brought to the retailer where it was bought.
Shoppers with questions about the recall can contact Grand Strand Sandwich at 843-399-2999 from Monday to Thursday between the hours of 8 p.m. and 4 p.m. and on Friday between 8 a.m. and 12 p.m.
This latest recall came just days after 2,414 other breakfast sandwiches were also recalled over listeria fears.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic staffer claims solution to mathematics’ Riemann hypothesis
articles.title_zh: Anthropic staffer claims solution to mathematics’ Riemann hypothesis
articles.content_orig:
The drama over AI in the math community is getting real.
Hours after Levent Alpöge , a mathematician at Anthropic, said he solved the most famous open problem in the field using AI on Friday, another mathematician came out of the woodwork to announce he'd also solved the problem.
Only this mathematician said he did it without using AI.
Alessandro Masullo, a postdoctoral researcher at Stanford, said he's been working on the problem for 12 years and was about a year away from releasing his results when he was blindsided by Alpöge's report.
"In light of the current climate I am being advised to release the current version as it is," he said in a paper posted online, adding that there may be errors in it because it was rushed.
And in a thinly veiled slight against Alpöge, who described working with Claude for weeks to reach his solution, Masullo said that human mathematicians still have a place in the age of AI.
"If any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here," he said. "We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere."
Masullo's solution, which is far shorter than Alpöge's, immediately sparked a further firestorm in a math community already reeling from the unprecedented Anthropic paper and months of AI companies announcing high-profile solutions to long-standing math problems.
"The plot thickens!" Steven Strogatz, a math professor at Cornell, said on X on Friday.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
"Now it's getting more complicated," Sergei Gukov, a math professor at Caltech , told Business Insider.
Mathematicians are now racing to scrutinize both solutions with their own brains and with AI. Neither had, by Friday afternoon, been formally proven.
At stake is nothing less than the credibility of human mathematicians in the age of AI, and who's solution is right will have grave implications for the future of mathematics.
Masullo, his partner at Stanford, Brian Conrad, and Alpöge did not respond to requests for comment on Friday.
The problem in question is the Riemann Hypothesis, which Strogatz described to Business Insider as the "White Whale" of mathematics. It proposes a predicted distribution for how often prime numbers appear alongside other numbers.
The task of proving the hypothesis is a Millennium Prize Problem , meaning that solving it earns a mathematician $1 million. The Navier-Stokes equations, which OpenAI has said it solved, are also in the Millennium Prize category.
Gukov, the math professor at Caltech, called the claim that it was solved a "HUGE deal."
"RH was the biggest problem in math," he said, using the past tense.

articles.title_orig: Google retiring Nest app and Google Assistant on speakers, displays in 2027
articles.title_zh: Google retiring Nest app and Google Assistant on speakers, displays in 2027
articles.content_orig:
Following the Android deprecation in September, Google Assistant is going away on speakers and smart displays next year. Additionally, Google Home is fully replacing the Nest app in January.
The Nest app on Android, iOS, and the web will stop working on January 25, 2027. The Google Home app, which requires a Google Account, will be needed to “continue controlling and receiving notifications from your Nest devices remotely.”
Officially, Google wants to “focus all of [its] engineering, security, and feature investments on one unified, modern experience.” It reiterated benefits like:
With home.nest.com going away, you have to download any custom video clips since they will not transfer over to Google Home. A one-click “Download All” button is available.
Terrible news. For all my first-gen Nest cameras (wired hello doorbell, wired outdoor cams, and multiple indoor cams), I vastly prefer the Nest app to the terrible Google Home app.
Otherwise, Nest app users do not need to do anything else, with devices automatically transferring over to the Google Home app. No Nest thermostats, cameras, doorbells, smoke alarms, or locks are losing support with this change.
Additionally, Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions will automatically switch to Google Home Premium “with no additional cost and no credit card re-entry required at this time.”
The other change announced today is that Google Assistant on speakers and smart displays is going away on August 2, 2027. It will be replaced by the Gemini for Home voice assistant. Google notes that natural language support replaces “rigid, static and highly specific voice commands.” Additionally:
You can upgrade to Gemini today , while Google is expanding international availability over the coming months. Google will share more updates closer to the deadline.
FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500 Is Set for Longest Losing Run Since 2020: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: S&P 500 Is Set for Longest Losing Run Since 2020: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Stocks were slammed on Friday, closing out a brutal week for markets as the much-hyped Anthropic IPO caused investors to take profits on the artificial intelligence-led rally rather than revive it. The Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year, and the S&P 500 entered correction territory alongside the Dow Jones Industrial Average .
The tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 4.3% and was down 1.7% year to date. The broad market S&P 500 traded down 2.9%, while the blue-chip Dow fell 573 points, or 1.2%. Both the S&P 500 and Dow were more than 10% below their closing records.
Anthropic lost 10%, giving back most of its 17% jump in its Nasdaq debut Thursday and pressuring the broader AI trade. Chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia slid 12% and more than 11%, respectively. Nvidia saw selling pressure increase after Reuters reported that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring possible accounting issues at the company. Micron Technology dropped more than 13%.
Those declines in tech built on the losses seen in Thursday's horrid session, where the major averages each losing more than 2%, and the Dow closing below the key 50,000 level for the first time since June.
"This is not just a valuation-driven correction. It's becoming broader," said Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon. "Right now, it's definitely risk-off."
The losses are alarming investors who were hopeful that Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's IPO would revive enthusiasm for the AI trade. Now, the market looks to be on the cusp of a true capitulation after getting roiled in recent weeks with a series of negative headlines. Signs of moderation in the capital expenditures splurge, Democratic wins in the 2026 midterms and Jensen Huang's ouster at Nvidia all raised questions about the future of the AI buildout.
On top of that, the potential for more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve is spooking traders as well.
Investors hid out in defensive areas of the market, with retailers such as Walmart and Costco as well as others like Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble seeing gains. Walmart gained 2%, while Costco, Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble each rose more than 1%.
"The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth," said Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners.
For the week, the Dow has fallen 7%, putting it on pace for its worst weekly performance since April 2025 in the wake of President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs announcement . The S&P 500 has decreased almost 8%, while the Nasdaq is down about 9%, with both also headed for their largest one-week pullbacks in more than a year.
Anthropic was the most-traded single stock by Vanguard's self-directed retail traders on Thursday, underscoring the buzz among mom-and-pop investors around the artificial intelligence leader's historic IPO.
Just about 0.2% of Vanguard's self-directed investors bought Anthropic on Thursday, which was its first day on the public market. These investors bought a median of 20 shares or roughly $1,950.
Vanguard said about around out of every 10 Anthropic buyers were men. By comparison, men account for 55% of Vanguard's investor base.
To be sure, Vanguard said a higher percentage of its base traded SpaceX during its public market debut session in June.
Anthropic jumped 17% in trading on Thursday after it went public. But the stock has dropped nearly 10% in afternoon trading Friday, which is its first full day on the market.
BTIG's chief market technician Jonathan Krinsky in an appearance on CNBC's " The Exchange " Friday pointed to technicals that make him think the sell-off isn't over just yet.
He specifically noted Apple , the largest stock by market cap, which is only down by 3% from its 2026 highs earlier this month. "When the S&P has been down at least 8% or more, when it's made its final bottom, the median drawdown for Apple has been 23%," he said. "It would be historically unprecedented to see a final bottom on the S&P with Apple where it is right now."
He added that 50% of the S&P 500's stocks are above their 50-day moving average, a level that is higher than a number closer to below 40% — or even 20% — when durable bottoms hit.
Krinsky did note, though, that relief for semiconductors may be coming, as the group is retreating to levels that it last traded at in early April when the group started to surge higher . The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) in late trading Friday was at levels it last closed below on April 9.
Anthropic debuted with a 17% advance on Thursday, starting off on the wrong foot as its performance came up short when compared with the day-one gains from other notable IPOs since last year.
The day-one moves of Circle , Figma , Cerebras and SpaceX all outdid Anthropic's, with Figma seeing the biggest jump at 250% .
Anthropic shares gave back much of that advance on Friday, falling more than 12% in afternoon trading.
President Donald Trump said on Friday that he wants to stop U.S. companies from building data centers in other countries.
"We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference. He added that companies would face tremendous penalties for building data centers abroad. "We want them to build it here."
He added that he is concerned about U.S. companies building in China instead. "We're not allowing that to happen," he said.
— Kevin Breuninger and Davis Giangiulio
The VIX volatility index , a gauge of how much the S&P 500 might move in the next 30 days based on options trading, rose another 13% intraday Friday to 32.27, after jumping as much as 16% Thursday, according to FactSet data.
The VIX, a gauge of skittishness on Wall Street, has now risen for six of the past seven days. The index hasn't closed above 30 since late March.
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook expressed caution about the dangers posed by inflation, saying Friday that if the central bank doesn't act now it risks having to do more later.
"Inflation has been above target for more than five and a half years, and every additional day poses greater risk that price- and wage-setters will adjust their inflation expectations upward," Cook said in remarks delivered in Chile.
"Furthermore, waiting longer to implement rate increases risks getting behind the curve," she added. "If we fall behind, additional and larger rate increases may be required later to catch up, which could increase stress on our financial system and have unnecessarily damaging effects on American households."
Cook was one of only two FOMC members who voted against the pause. Markets strongly expect the committee to approve a quarter percentage point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting.
The tech selling intensified in late-morning trading, with the sector down more than 5% on the day. That decline pushed its week-to-date losses to 10.5% as of 11:57 a.m. ET. That would be tech's biggest one-week drop since April 4, 2025, when the Trump administration announced massive tariffs on imported products.
The Nasdaq Composite dropped Friday, turning negative for 2026, as even Anthropic's IPO and Nvidia's earnings failed to revive the artificial intelligence trade. The tech-heavy index was last lower by 2.6% for the trading session, falling slightly on the year.
Bitcoin slid more than 4% with the broader market, falling below the $60,000 level for the first time since July.
The flagship cryptocurrency was last trading at $59,554.95 and is now heading for a retest its July low of $57,737.35.
Ether fell 6% to $1,650.79, its lowest level since July 2.
The outlook for consumers improved in November as expectations for inflation eased, according to a University of Michigan survey Friday.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin Seek to Project Power at Their First Summit
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin Seek to Project Power at Their First Summit
articles.content_orig:
It was the first-ever meeting of the leaders of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers—one that host Xi Jinping opened by hailing its “pioneering significance.”
Exactly what was achieved when Xi met with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump at Kylin Villa in northwestern Shenzhen on Thursday, however, has onlookers scratching their heads. Xi started by invoking the responsibility of Great Powers toward world peace; Putin delved into historic “shared interests;” while Trump immediately lashed out at “rogue globalist organisations,” such as the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The ICC “has gotten out of control,” Trump told his companions seated around a round wooden table, and has “really strayed far beyond its jurisdiction.”
It was almost as if this historic trilateral , held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, didn’t have any fixed agenda. It hadn’t. When the confab was first proposed, Putin wanted to talk about Ukraine, though U.S. officials pushed back. Trump instead suggested nuclear arms and Iran, but Beijing wasn’t keen. Finally, China’s Foreign Ministry settled on “safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations.”
It was therefore an occasion rich with platitudes but not a lot else. “In this global village, major countries shoulder special responsibilities,” said Xi, who also called for the destruction of all nuclear weapons. “Positive interaction among major powers is not an optional question, but a compulsory one.”
Still, the meeting served its purpose. Trump gained a chance to project influence after chastening midterms and the unfolding Nvidia saga that forced the resignation of his close friend Jensen Huang as CEO. Xi got to flaunt himself as the consummate statesman, while Putin took a baby step out from the diplomatic cold. But it was also a distinctly unsettling sight for the U.S. President to be sitting beside two of America’s most consequential adversaries, whose governments declared in 2022 that their friendship with each other had “no limits.”
Before the three-way meeting, Trump met separately with Putin and then Xi. His roughly 40 minutes with the Russian President began on a hopeful note: “Wonderful things can come out of this—or at least start,” Trump said. During an hour of talks with Xi, Trump returned to a more familiar concern. “I’ll be asking you to do some more for our farmers,” he said. He also suggested that Washington and Beijing could work together to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.
That prospect mattered to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said Wednesday that the war could end in a single meeting if the U.S. and China used their economic leverage against Moscow. Instead, Trump launched a broadside against the ICC, which has issued an arrest warrant against Putin for war crimes, urging his autocratic counterparts to cooperate on “ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty.”
Trump also said it was “vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world,” before segueing into a justification of his war in Iran : “That’s what we’re doing in Iran. We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Of course, this was always going to be an occasion that would put style over substance. On Wednesday, Xi surprised onlookers by greeting a clearly delighted Trump on the tarmac at Shenzhen Baoan Airport. Their handshake turned into a brief hug, before five People’s Liberation Army J-10C fighter jets flew overhead, billowing red, yellow, and blue smoke.
In personally meeting Trump as he deplaned Air Force One, Xi reciprocated the welcome he received from the U.S. President at Joint Base Andrews in September. The gesture was a first by a top Chinese leader since Mao Zedong met Nikita Khrushchev at Beijing’s airport in 1959.
Putin had to suffice with being greeted by Xi’s chief of staff, Cai Qi, upon his earlier arrival in the wee hours of Wednesday morning. But Xi spent much of that afternoon in talks with his embattled Russian counterpart, who used his speech to assembled CEOs to lambast Western sanctions, crowing that the U.S. and Europe had “punished themselves” with punitive measures, which Russia had successfully sidestepped anyway.
Upon emerging from his two-hour bilateral with Putin, Xi called on both countries to “lead and advance … the democratization of international relations.” Putin, in turn, boasted that economic coercion was “a thing of the past.” Later in the evening, Putin and Trump shook hands before the gala dinner as Xi looked on smiling.
“Beijing’s top priority would be to create a more stable external environment for China’s development, particularly by making relations with Washington more predictable while maintaining steady cooperation with Moscow,” says Sun Chenghao, a fellow with Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy.
Still, the summit threatened to be overshadowed by the Nvidia scandal, with company founder Huang admitting an affair with a woman accused of illicitly funneling chips to China and whom U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly suspect may be a Chinese spy. On Nov. 16, the U.S. Commerce Department issued an interim rule aimed at stopping Chinese firms from accessing advanced U.S. chips through data centers abroad.
Trump told Fox News that he and Xi “spoke the whole evening” during Wednesday’s gala dinner but only “briefly” discussed Nvidia. Trump also claimed he was unaware of the espionage allegations, which China vehemently denies. “I haven’t heard that she was a spy,” Trump said. “She was a businesswoman who bought chips, and who knows if they were bought right or wrong.”
Trump also appeared to shoot down any hopes of regulation governing AI: “We oppose any form of globalist regulation or anything to control or stifle [AI], and we won’t allow that to happen,” he said.
Still, the historic trilateral did succeed in visibly placing China at the center of Great Power diplomacy. Hosting the leaders alongside APEC supports Beijing’s claim that global influence is shifting eastward, with China as a stabilizing power, particularly amid unpredictable U.S. policy.
“The optics might actually play well for China,” says Chong Ja Ian, a professor of international relations at the National University of Singapore. “It certainly would fit the sort of image that Beijing and Xi would like to create for themselves.”
But while APEC was created in 1989 to ease trade and investment across the region, today’s world has been gripped by rising protectionism. The Trump Administration has levied tariffs on 60 trading partners that together account for 99.4% of U.S. imports, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. Moreover, Europe is increasingly chary about cheap Chinese exports that Brussels says are fueled by subsidies and industrial overcapacity.
Xi used his Wednesday address to business leaders to promise a more open Chinese market and present the world’s second-largest economy as a source of opportunity. “History tells us that opening doors brings progress while closing doors leaves one behind,” he said.
Yet the image of three elderly leaders debating global problems behind closed doors sits uneasily beside Xi’s call for a more multipolar world. Pro-Kremlin media was especially keen to frame the meeting as Yalta 2.0 after the historic powwow between Roosevelt, Stalin, and Churchill toward the end of World War II.
But it is Ukraine’s plucky defiance of Putin's invasion that underscores how today’s Middle Powers have more agency. At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney urged third countries to work together on trade, security and technology in order to shape the rules and resist economic coercion. “Middle powers must act together because if you are not at the table, you are on the menu,” Carney said.

articles.title_orig: Myanmar calls UN court's Rohingya genocide ruling a 'great disappointment'
articles.title_zh: Myanmar calls UN court's Rohingya genocide ruling a 'great disappointment'
articles.content_orig:
A Rohingya refugee waves Myanmar's national flag as he waits for the arrival of U.N. General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman at a refugee camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 20, 2026.
The world’s top international court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority, more than a million of whom remain displaced.
The verdict , issued Thursday, is the first time a state has been found responsible for committing genocide in the history of the International Court of Justice, which was established in 1945. In a weekslong military campaign in 2017, Myanmar forces killed at least 10,000 people, including up to 2,109 children under five, and forced more than 700,000 others to flee the country’s northern Rakhine State.
The landmark decision could have significant implications for the legal treatment of cases brought under the 1948 Genocide Convention, Melanie O’Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia Law School, tells TIME. That includes South Africa’s pending case alleging that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza , where Israeli forces have killed tens of thousands of people over the past three years.
A spokesperson for Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing told reporters on Friday that the ruling is “unfair.” Min Aung Hlaing was the military’s commander in chief during the 2017 operation.
“It was not a decision made unanimously,” spokesperson Khine Khine Soe said, pointing out that six of the 15 judges dissented. She did not say whether Myanmar would comply with the ruling.
Myanmar’s military junta-backed government denied committing genocide during the proceedings.
Read More: Myanmar’s Dictator Wants to Rebuild Ties With the West
The National Unity Government, a parallel government formed after Myanmar’s 2021 military coup, said on Thursday that it respects the judgment.
For the Rohingya, the ruling is “public acknowledgment in a court of law and in the top court in the world that what happened to them was genocide,” says O’Brien, who has published multiple books on genocide and international criminal law, is working on a book about the Genocide Convention in the ICJ.
Members of the Rohingya community also said the ruling is a historic recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group.
“Myanmar denies the existence of the Rohingya,” Sayed Ullah, a community leader at a refugee camp in Bangladesh, told the Associated Press , “but now the court made it clear.”
The court’s finding of genocide by a state is a historic first. Two previous genocide cases brought before the ICJ have gone to the merit stages, both arising from the wars that followed the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s.
In 2007, the court ruled on a case brought by Bosnia against Serbia. The court determined that the killing of thousands of Bosniak men and boys in Srebrenica in 1995 was genocide, but it found insufficient evidence to attribute the killings by Bosnian Serb forces to Serbia. Still, the court ruled that Serbia violated its obligation under the Genocide Convention by failing to use its influence over those forces to prevent genocide.
In the second case, which was brought by Croatia against Serbia, the court made no finding that genocide was committed. It instead ruled in a 2015 judgment that Yugoslav army and Serb forces had an intent to ethnically cleanse Croats from Serb-held areas of Croatia, forcing between 80,000 and 100,000 Croats and other non-Serbs to flee the Krajina region between April 1991 and April 1992.
“The Court has not rewritten or expanded the legal definition of genocide” since the earlier cases, Marko Milanovic, a professor of public international law at the University of Reading, said in a statement . “What it has done is take a more flexible approach to the evidence used to establish genocide, particularly the notoriously difficult question of proving genocidal intent.”
The dissenting judges argued that the evidence could support the intent of forced expulsion or collective punishment instead of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group.
The court ordered Myanmar’s military-backed government to ensure the safe, voluntary return of the Rohingya to the country and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.
Myanmar has two years to report to the ICJ on its orders of restitution. If it is unable to carry out restitution, the court ordered the government to pay reparations to the Rohingya, the amount of which will be determined at a later stage.
It’s uncertain whether Myanmar will implement the ruling, which is legally binding.
“Therein lies the rub in that there isn’t necessarily a mechanism for enforcing them,” says O’Brien. If Myanmar does not comply, The Gambia, which brought the case to the ICJ, can turn to the United Nations Security Council, which has discretion over whether to act, although China, which has veto power as a member of the council, is friendly to the Myanmar government.
Third party states can also exert pressure on Myanmar to comply with the ruling, such as through direct diplomatic pressure or sanctions on individuals or companies linked to the genocide. On Thursday, the U.K. ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defense attaché and called for an urgent U.N. Security Council meeting to discuss the judgment. ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights (APHR), an independent group of current and former Southeast Asian parliamentarians, called on the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to support implementation of the ruling. Cheah Wui Ling, an associate professor at the National University of Singapore’s faculty of law, says ASEAN is obligated to “act in ways that respect and not undermine” the ruling, given the organization’s commitment to international law.
Cheah says the ruling could give “fresh momentum” to efforts seeking to hold individuals criminally accountable for the genocide, including an investigation in Argentina and a criminal complaint in Indonesia .
The prosecutor at the International Criminal Court also requested an arrest warrant in 2024 for Min Aung Hlaing. The ruling could have a “snowball effect” on that investigation, says Vincent-Joël Proulx, an associate professor at National University of Singapore’s faculty of law and a former special adviser to the ICJ’s president.
Even so, other challenges remain to seeing restitution through, O’Brien says.
Nine years after the mass displacement, more than a million Rohingya refugees live in Bangladesh, with most in camps in Cox’s Bazar. Some refugees told the AP that they want to return home to Myanmar.
Read More: ‘There Is No Hope’: Death and Desperation Take Over the World’s Largest Refugee Camp
Rohingya refugees visit a market at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 17, 2026. Salahuddin Ahmed—AFP/Getty Images
But many of those homes and villages were completely destroyed, O’Brien says. “They have nothing physically to come back to.” She adds that the Rohingya have faced “decades of discrimination and persecution,” and it’s “very difficult to suddenly turn around a culture of hostility and discrimination.”
Restitution is “trying to put the victims in the position that they were in before this had happened,” says O’Brien. But “so many of them have lost family members, and so many of them have been subject to horrific violence and abuse, so they can’t be put in exactly the same position.”
Eyes are now on South Africa’s genocide case against Israel. The case is in a second round of written pleadings and is expected to take at least three more years.
Myanmar’s defense argued that its military operations targeted militants, not civilians. But the court considered a broader “pattern of conduct” by Myanmar, including hate speech, discriminatory laws, displacement, destruction of property, and widespread sexual violence.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
articles.title_zh: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
articles.content_orig:
An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.
An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.
Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website , Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday .
The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:
I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof 1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.
The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August , but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”
Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules , a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”
In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture , a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.
OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.
OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar.
Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Scandal: Timeline That Led To His Resignation—And Potential Comeback
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Scandal: Timeline That Led To His Resignation—And Potential Comeback
articles.content_orig:
Author of the AI Insider newsletter
It's rare that investors get a chance to put a clear dollar value on a CEO .
With Jensen Huang , we just got one. And it's an astonishing number: $1 trillion.
That's how much Nvidia has lost in market value since Huang was forced out of the AI chip giant last week.
It's potentially a terrible look for Nvidia's board of directors .
After all, the fundamental job of a public company's board is to look after the interests of shareholders. That doesn't mean maximizing the stock price every day, or keeping a CEO at all costs. Directors have broader legal duties and sometimes must make difficult decisions that hurt investors in the short term.
But when a board oversees the departure of a CEO and shareholders subsequently lose $1 trillion, it's reasonable to ask whether the directors have fulfilled their most important responsibility.
On November 11, the day before Nvidia announced Huang's departure, the company's shares closed at $173.73, giving it a market value of about $4.2 trillion.
By Friday afternoon, the stock had fallen to roughly $128, wiping out more than a quarter of Nvidia's market value.
According to Bloomberg data, the company's market capitalization has shrunk to about $3.14 trillion since Huang was ousted. That's a staggering $1.04 trillion decline in just over a week.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Of course, stock prices move for all sorts of reasons. And it's impossible to attribute every dollar of that decline to Huang's departure.
But here's what makes this particularly interesting.
Much of the bad news surrounding Nvidia was already out in the open before Huang left.
The original New York Times story about Nvidia's dealings with Megaspeed and his relationship with Alice Huang was published in October 2025 — more than a year ago .
And the unconfirmed allegation that she might be a Chinese spy was reported on Oct. 29, a full two weeks before Huang's ouster.
Those worries had already pushed Nvidia shares down substantially.
Then Huang was gone early on Nov. 12. From that point on, Nvidia's share price became mostly a referendum on the man himself.
Suddenly investors were looking at something very different: Nvidia without the visionary founder who built it into the world's dominant AI chip company.
That's a particularly unsettling prospect in technology, where the person at the top can have an extraordinary influence on which products get built, which bets get made, and where an entire industry goes next.
Does Nvidia's board believe it acted in shareholders' best interests? How does it assess the enormous decline in market value since Huang left? I asked Nvidia's press office these questions on Friday and haven't got an answer yet.
There are plenty of ways to value a company. Revenue. Profits. Growth prospects.
But sometimes the market gives us a rare glimpse of something harder to measure: The value of one person.

articles.title_orig: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B
articles.title_zh: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B
articles.content_orig:
Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.
Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.
Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares.
Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.
Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the company has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro . Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.
“We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July .

articles.title_orig: Trump says Iran wants a deal, Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis exchange fire and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Trump says Iran wants a deal, Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis exchange fire and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, headquarters of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund , was struck on Thursday in a Houthi attack in the latest blow to the kingdom in its war with the Iran-backed Yemeni group.
Saudi Arabia’s civil defense said a Houthi attack on a tower in Riyadh’s financial center caused material damage to several floors of the building and nearby buildings, but no injuries were reported , state news agency SPA said. The statement did not identify the tower, but an accompanying photograph published by SPA showed the PIF Tower.
The Houthis said they had targeted Riyadh’s financial center twice on Thursday, first at dawn and again in the evening.
They also said they had attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Khamis Mushait airbase in southern Saudi Arabia and SADAF Petrochemical Company in Jubail in the kingdom’s Eastern Province. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of these attacks.
The kingdom’s foreign ministry said it reserved the right to take “all necessary measures” to defend its sovereignty and protect its citizens and national assets following the Houthi attack.
The strike blew out windows across seven to eight floors of the PIF Tower, bending parts of its metal facade . It was the second time in less than two weeks that a Houthi attack damaged a landmark in Riyadh’s financial district, with state oil company Aramco’s building hit in a November 8 attack.
The King Abdullah Financial District was closed to visitors following the attack.
Three sources familiar with the matter said the building had been struck by an incoming Houthi missile . The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had “dealt with a missile threat” launched towards Riyadh and that debris had fallen.
PIF, which stands for the Public Investment Fund, acknowledged receiving a Reuters request for comment. The Houthis issued no immediate statement on the strike.
The Houthis have been firing at Saudi airports and oil infrastructure since Yemen’s frozen civil war reignited in July amid the US-Iran war. On the ground in Yemen, the group has seized swathes of territory from the Saudi-backed government, forcing it to stage a major retreat at the weekend.
Residents of the Saudi capital were awoken by a loud boom in the early hours of Thursday.
Saudi Arabia’s civil defense issued several warnings of potential danger in Riyadh throughout Thursday, including after the attack, before announcing that the threat had passed.
The Houthi-run Saba news agency reported that Saudi aircraft had carried out airstrikes on the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital Sanaa early on Thursday, without providing further details.
Saudi authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the strikes.
The conflict has dealt a blow to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s plans to develop and diversify the economy of Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter and a US ally.
The prince met US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper in Riyadh on Wednesday, Cooper’s third publicly reported visit to Saudi Arabia since the Yemen conflict resumed.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that Saudi officials now foresee the campaign stretching on for up to six months , according to two Western officials briefed by the Saudis on the kingdom’s plans. A third ​source familiar with the Saudi plans confirmed the accounts.
The sources said the Saudis, who replaced the commander of their coalition fighting in Yemen this week, want to see their allies make gains on the ground before they enter any negotiations with the Houthis.
Meanwhile, the situation in Yemen has appeared to favour the Houthis, who have seized Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast including the strategically vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait at its mouth, and have surrounded the city of Taiz in highlands overlooking the government’s temporary capital Aden.
In the wider war, which began in February when the United States and Israel attacked Iran , there has been no sign of a breakthrough in negotiations mediated by Qatar.
Meanwhile, there has been an uptick in hostilities in the Gulf in recent days, with Iran firing at US allies Bahrain and Kuwait and US airstrikes hitting Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.
Saudi Arabia first entered the Yemen conflict in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to restore Yemen’s government to power ​after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country. They fought to a bloody stalemate and in 2022 reached a ceasefire that lasted until summer this year.

articles.title_orig: Poland condemns Russian 'provocation' after three airspace violations
articles.title_zh: Poland condemns Russian 'provocation' after three airspace violations
articles.content_orig:
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".
In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".
European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.
Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
